project.name: ruby-gba
project.description: A Ruby DSL that compiles plain Ruby into real Game Boy Advance ROM files (pure Ruby, no C extensions). Built as a teaching tool: the user is assumed to know Ruby but not GBA hardware, so the framework manages VRAM, DMA, palettes, display modes and VBlank timing, and turns the classic silent-black-screen footguns into friendly build-time errors. Programs are built as a target-agnostic IR that is validated by guardrails and then lowered either to an ARM7 ROM or to a headless Ruby interpreter used as a test oracle.

nodes.name: animate.rb
nodes.summary: Runnable example that builds a bitmap-screen ROM where a spinning gold coin is steered around a field with the D-pad. It showcases flipbook animation: a sprite given a `frames:` list and a `rate:` cycles its pictures automatically while still responding to `move`.
nodes.languageNotes: The four coin frames are generated at build time by a Ruby ellipse formula rather than hand-drawn ASCII art, so the whole spin is one small method.

nodes.name: Animate
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the spinning-coin demo: the frame-width table, the generated coin art, and the `RubyGBA.game` block that assembles the ROM.

nodes.name: coin_art
nodes.summary: Generates one animation frame as ASCII art — a gold disc squashed horizontally to that frame's width — so cycling the four frames reads as a coin turning edge-on and back.

nodes.name: gen_pacman_sheet.rb
nodes.summary: Build-time asset generator that bakes the Pac-Man disc-and-mouth formula into a real PNG sprite sheet (one row per direction, two columns for mouth open and shut) using ImageMagick. It is the authoring step for the sheet that `examples/pacman.rb` imports with `facing_from:`.
nodes.languageNotes: Packs the sheet as raw RGBA bytes with a fully transparent background, so the importer's `transparent: true` cut-out works without a separate mask.

nodes.name: bird.rb
nodes.summary: Runnable example that imports a sprite straight from a native `.aseprite` file with `from_aseprite:` — no export step — and flies the six-frame flapping bird around the sky with the D-pad.
nodes.languageNotes: Demonstrates the modern art workflow: the framework reads the artist's saved file directly, compositing layers and resolving the palette at build time.

nodes.name: Bird
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the Aseprite-import demo's game definition — the screen, the imported bird sprite, and the D-pad steering loop.

nodes.name: breakout.rb
nodes.summary: The bitmap-mode flagship showcase: a complete Breakout with a brick wall, angle-steering paddle bounces, scoring, three lives, a title screen and a game-over screen. It is drawn tear-free (double-buffered) because every frame repaints the whole field.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately steers plain variables with draw_rect_at instead of sprites: when a game clears and repaints every frame there is no background for a save-under sprite to preserve.

nodes.name: Breakout
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the whole Breakout game definition — layout constants, sound effects, the brick wall, and the title, playing and game-over scenes wired through a state variable.

nodes.name: buffered_bounce.rb
nodes.summary: Minimal tear-free demo: three balls bounce around while the whole screen is cleared and repainted every frame. It exists to show that `tear_free: true` is the single flag that makes the naive redraw-everything style safe.

nodes.name: BufferedBounce
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the bouncing-balls game definition: per-ball position and velocity variables plus the clear-and-repaint frame loop.

nodes.name: floating_digits.rb
nodes.summary: Example where the digits 0 through 9 drift around the screen and bounce off the walls, each in its own color. It teaches the difference between a number that changes value in place (draw_number) and one whose position moves, which must be blitted as a glyph image.

nodes.name: FloatingDigits
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the drifting-digits demo: it turns each built-in font glyph into a small image and moves and blits the ten digits every frame.

nodes.name: font_styles.rb
nodes.summary: Example that draws the same word in three fonts — the built-in 5x7 default plus a rounded lowercase font and a slanted script font defined inline with `font :name do glyph … end`.

nodes.name: FontStyles
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the font demo: two custom fonts declared from glyph bitmap art, then the same word drawn once per font.

nodes.name: fonts.rb
nodes.summary: Small example that draws the same score twice — once in the built-in 5x7 `:default` font and once in the compact 3x5 `:tiny` font — to show per-text font selection through the `font:` argument.

nodes.name: FontsDemo
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the two-font comparison: one screen that draws a label and a number in each registered font.

nodes.name: grid_cursor.rb
nodes.summary: Example that steers one lit cell around a board with the D-pad, leaving no trail. It shows what `grid` is for: the game talks in cell coordinates and only the two cells that change are repainted each move.

nodes.name: GridCursor
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the grid-cursor demo: the board declaration plus the per-frame clear_cell / set_cell move in cell coordinates.

nodes.name: hero.rb
nodes.summary: Example of the follow-you camera almost every adventure game uses: a hero sprite stays pinned to the middle of the screen while a tiled world larger than the screen scrolls underneath, and the world wraps as a torus.
nodes.languageNotes: Combines a hardware sprite with a scrolling background — the console composites the hero over the moving scenery for free, so nothing smears or tears.

nodes.name: Hero
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the follow-cam demo: the tileset and world map, the centered hero sprite, and the per-frame `scroll_to` that points the camera at the hero's world position.

nodes.name: jukebox.rb
nodes.summary: The sound showcase: a small music player listing three classical tunes, where UP and DOWN move a cursor and the highlighted piece plays and loops. All three melodies are written with the note-and-tempo `song` DSL.

nodes.name: Jukebox
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the music-player demo: three `song` definitions, the selectable track list, and the bobbing blocks that show something is playing.

nodes.name: level.rb
nodes.summary: Example that draws a level designed in a map editor rather than typed into the code: `tiles from:` cuts a whole PNG sheet into numbered tiles and `background from:` reads a Tiled-exported CSV tilemap, with tile 1 marked solid so the hero cannot cross it.

nodes.name: Level
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the CSV-tilemap demo: the imported numbered tileset, the map loaded from file, and a hero blocked by the solid tiles.

nodes.name: maze.rb
nodes.summary: Example that walks a hero through corridors it cannot leave. It demonstrates tile collision: mark wall tiles with `solid:` in the tileset, declare the sprite `blocked_by` the background, and the framework checks every step — stopping at walls and sliding along them.
nodes.languageNotes: Also shows the escape hatch: `can_move?` asks before moving, while raw `move_to` and x/y writes are never collision-checked.

nodes.name: Maze
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the wall-collision demo: the tileset with its solid wall character, the maze map, and the hero wired to be blocked by the background.

nodes.name: pacman.rb
nodes.summary: The tiled-mode flagship showcase: a Pac-Man that eats pellets and is chased by a ghost, putting the whole tile-plus-hardware-sprite stack together — a tiled background room, hardware sprites, per-direction `facing:` poses, sprite-to-sprite collision, a score HUD and sound.
nodes.languageNotes: The four Pac poses are generated from a disc-and-wedge formula rather than drawn; rotating to an arbitrary angle would need the console's affine hardware.

nodes.name: Pacman
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the Pac-Man game definition plus the art formula: the room tileset and map, the facing sprite, the pellet and ghost sprites, collision handling and sound.

nodes.name: pacman_art
nodes.summary: Generates Pac-Man's ASCII art for one facing direction — a yellow disc with a wedge bitten out on the side he faces — so the four poses come from a formula instead of hand-drawn frames.

nodes.name: in_mouth?
nodes.summary: Decides whether a pixel offset from Pac-Man's center falls inside the mouth wedge for a given facing direction, which is what carves the bite out of the disc.

nodes.name: parallax.rb
nodes.summary: Example that stacks two tiled background layers and scrolls them at different speeds to fake depth: a far sky with drifting clouds behind a near ground layer whose see-through tiles let the sky show through.
nodes.languageNotes: Layer order comes from declaration order — the first background declared is the backmost — so nothing in the game code names a hardware layer or a priority.

nodes.name: Parallax
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the parallax demo: the sky and ground tilesets and maps, and the frame loop that scrolls the near layer twice as fast as the far one.

nodes.name: piano.rb
nodes.summary: The sampled-audio showcase: two animated hands play a tune, the right hand carrying the melody while the left vamps a block chord, so three notes sound together. A single recorded piano sample is re-pitched across the keyboard by `instrument` and summed by the software mixer.
nodes.languageNotes: Proves polyphony from one recording: each note becomes a pitched voice in the mixer instead of a synthesized PSG tone.

nodes.name: Piano
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the two-hand piano demo: the imported hand and key art, the recorded note loaded as an instrument, and the score that drives the finger animation and the chords.

nodes.name: pixels.rb
nodes.summary: The simplest example: a ROM that draws single pixels and filled rectangles on a direct-color bitmap screen (an Italian flag). It is the smallest complete program the DSL can produce.

nodes.name: pong.rb
nodes.summary: Single-player Pong against a CPU paddle, first to five points, with a title screen, background music during play and sound effects on paddle hits, wall bounces and scoring. Written as a top-level script rather than a namespaced module.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses `approach` to move the CPU paddle toward the ball a capped step at a time, which is how the framework expresses simple AI without per-frame branching.

nodes.name: raycaster.rb
nodes.summary: A first-person 3D view of a small maze drawn the way Wolfenstein 3D was: one ray per screen column, with the wall column's height derived from the hit distance. It is really a showcase for `table` — sine, reciprocal heights and the maze grid are precomputed in Ruby at build time and shipped as read-only ROM lookups.
nodes.languageNotes: The console cannot do sine or division cheaply per ray per frame, so the curves move to build time; the remaining bottleneck is painting each wall column one row at a time, holding it near 20 frames a second.

nodes.name: Raycaster
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the raycaster: the build-time sine, height and world tables, and the per-column ray-marching loop that paints the view.

nodes.name: scroll.rb
nodes.summary: Example that pans a camera around a 32x32-tile world larger than the screen using `scroll_by`. It shows the background as a torus — scroll far enough and the map wraps — which is the groundwork the follow-you camera is built on.

nodes.name: Scroll
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the camera-panning demo: the tileset, the oversized world map, and the D-pad loop that slides the visible window.

nodes.name: sheet.rb
nodes.summary: Example that brings art in from PNG files instead of typing it out: `tiles from:` cuts a tile sheet so each map character points at a cell, and `sprite frames_from:` cuts a sprite sheet into walk-cycle frames — with no intermediate build step.

nodes.name: Sheet
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the PNG-import demo: an imported tileset with an inline room map, and an animated hero sliced from a sprite sheet.

nodes.name: snake.rb
nodes.summary: The classic Snake, built to show the pieces of a real game: `list` for the growing body, `seed`/`rand` for the food, `every` for the movement beat, a live `draw_number` score, and scenes wired through a state variable.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately draws incrementally — repainting only the new head, the old head and the vacated tail — because redrawing the whole board would not fit in the console's brief safe window once the snake grows long.

nodes.name: Snake
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the whole Snake game definition: the body lists, the movement beat, food placement, collision rules and the title, playing and game-over scenes.

nodes.name: snake_buffered.rb
nodes.summary: The same Snake game written the naive way — clear the screen and repaint everything every frame — which stays clean only because the screen is double-buffered. It is the deliberate counterpart to `examples/snake.rb` and exists to show what `tear_free: true` buys you.

nodes.name: BufferedSnake
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the double-buffered Snake: the same rules and scenes as the incremental version, but with a full clear-and-repaint frame loop.

nodes.name: sprite_mover.rb
nodes.summary: Example that steers a hand-drawn heart around the screen with the D-pad to introduce the software `sprite`: it remembers the pixels underneath itself and paints them back, so the frame loop needs no `clear_screen` and no `blit`.

nodes.name: SpriteMover
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the save-under sprite demo: the field painted once up front, the heart image, and a loop that only changes the sprite's x and y.

nodes.name: tiles.rb
nodes.summary: Example that draws a static room out of four reusable 8x8 tiles stamped onto a grid by a character map. It is the introduction to tiled backgrounds: a tile is just an `image`, a tileset maps characters to tiles, and `background` paints the grid.

nodes.name: Tiles
nodes.summary: Namespace module holding the static tiled-room demo: four hand-drawn tile images, the tileset that names them, and the room map that stamps them.

nodes.name: ruby_gba.rb
nodes.summary: The library entry point: a require barrel pulling in all 40 modules of the framework, plus `RubyGBA.build`, the single call that turns a DSL block into a finished ROM. Every example and tool requires this one file.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby's `require_relative` list doubles as the load order, so files that define constants other files reference (constants, color, IR) are required before their consumers.

nodes.name: build
nodes.summary: The whole compile pipeline in one call: evaluates the user's DSL block into an IR tree, verifies the tree is well-formed, runs the guardrails and reports friendly findings (fatal ones stop the build), lowers the tree with the GBA backend, and assembles the result into a validated cartridge.
nodes.languageNotes: Separates two failure kinds: an IR verification failure is a library bug and raises loudly, while a guardrail finding is a plain-language message to the game author, printed advisory or fatal.

nodes.name: aseprite.rb
nodes.summary: The Aseprite importer, which lets a game point straight at the file a pixel artist saved. It parses Aseprite's JSON sheet export into plain data and decodes the native binary `.aseprite` format directly — layers, cels, palette, frame durations and named animations (frameTags).
nodes.languageNotes: The named animations are the real value over a blind grid slice: the artist's `walk` and `attack` tags become animations the game plays by name.

nodes.name: Aseprite
nodes.summary: Module holding the Aseprite import surface: the immutable value objects for frames, tags, documents and decoded sprites, plus the JSON parsing and binary loading entry points.

nodes.name: Decoder
nodes.summary: Reads the native `.aseprite` binary byte by byte: walks the frame and chunk headers, decompresses cel pixel data, resolves the indexed palette, composites the layers with their opacity, and collects the named animation tags.

nodes.name: parse
nodes.summary: Parses an Aseprite JSON sheet export into a plain document — the PNG filename it names, the ordered frame rectangles with their durations, and the named animations — accepting both the array and hash frame layouts Aseprite can write.

nodes.name: load_binary
nodes.summary: Entry point for reading a native `.aseprite` file: hands the raw bytes to the Decoder and returns the fully decoded sprite with its frames and named animations.

nodes.name: sprite
nodes.summary: Drives the whole binary decode: iterates the file's frames, composites every visible layer's cel onto a canvas, records each frame's duration, and returns the finished sprite with its tags.

nodes.name: paint_cel
nodes.summary: Walks one frame's chunks and paints each cel onto the frame canvas in layer order, skipping hidden layers and applying each layer's opacity.

nodes.name: read_cel
nodes.summary: Reads a single cel chunk — its position, size and pixel data — decompressing the zlib-packed variant so both raw and compressed cel types come back as plain pixels.

nodes.name: blit_cel
nodes.summary: Composites one cel's pixels onto the canvas at its offset, blending against what is already there according to the layer opacity and leaving see-through pixels untouched.

nodes.name: pixel_color
nodes.summary: Turns one source pixel into a console color, handling Aseprite's RGBA, grayscale and indexed color depths and marking fully transparent pixels as see-through.

nodes.name: read_palette
nodes.summary: Reads the file's palette chunk into a lookup table, so indexed-color frames can resolve each pixel index to an actual color.

nodes.name: read_tags
nodes.summary: Reads the frameTags chunk into named animations — each tag's name and its inclusive from/to frame range — which is what lets a game call `sprite.play(:walk)`.

nodes.name: asm.rb
nodes.summary: The ARM (ARMv4T) instruction encoder: each method returns raw 32-bit little-endian bytes for one instruction. Only the subset the backend needs is implemented — branches, data processing, loads and stores, shifts, stack ops and software interrupts.
nodes.languageNotes: ARM has no general 32-bit immediate: a constant must be an 8-bit value rotated by an even amount, which is why loading an arbitrary number takes a multi-instruction fallback.

nodes.name: ASM
nodes.summary: Module of ARM instruction encoders plus the condition-code constants that conditional branches and moves are built from.

nodes.name: return
nodes.summary: Encodes the subroutine return used by every DSL `func` — popping the saved link register straight into the program counter so the call and return stay one matched pair.

nodes.name: load_immediate
nodes.summary: Loads any 32-bit constant into a register, choosing the cheapest encoding available: a single rotated-immediate move where the value allows it, the inverted form via MVN, or a build-up of several instructions when neither fits.

nodes.name: load_immediate_fixed
nodes.summary: Loads a 32-bit constant using a fixed, always-the-same number of instructions, so the two-pass jump math can compute branch offsets before the constants are known.

nodes.name: mov_imm_cond
nodes.summary: Encodes a conditional move of a small constant, which is how comparisons become 0/1 values without a branch.

nodes.name: encode_rotated_immediate
nodes.summary: Tries to express a value as ARM's 8-bit-value-plus-even-rotation immediate, returning the packed field when it fits and nil when it does not — the test the other encoders branch on.

nodes.name: background.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the handle the `background` verb returns: a scrollable tiled background whose visible window is moved with `scroll_by` / `scroll_to`. It also exposes the tileset's solid tiles as collision boxes for sprites that are `blocked_by` it.
nodes.languageNotes: The map is a torus — scroll past an edge and it wraps — so a map only needs to be as large as the pattern that repeats, and no scroll register is ever named at the surface.

nodes.name: Background
nodes.summary: The scrollable-background handle: tracks the window's top-left corner in two hidden variables and records the scroll operations into the IR as the game calls them.

nodes.name: solid_boxes
nodes.summary: Returns the tileset's solid tiles as merged collision Boxes, which is what a sprite tests against when it is told to be blocked by this background.

nodes.name: scroll_by
nodes.summary: Slides the visible window by a relative amount in pixels — the usual way to scroll as the player moves — accepting numbers or runtime expression Values.

nodes.name: scroll_to
nodes.summary: Puts the visible window's top-left corner at an exact map position, which is how a follow-you camera snaps to the character each frame.

nodes.name: bounds.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the rectangle-bounds contract for collision: anything that can answer left, top, right and bottom gains `overlaps?` and the screen-edge tests by mixing this in. It is why `hero.overlaps?(coin)` works with no boxes declared.
nodes.languageNotes: The tests return Conditions rather than booleans, so they compose with the same expression sugar as any comparison and branch through `.then`.

nodes.name: Bounds
nodes.summary: The mixin that turns four edge readers into a full collision surface — rectangle overlap plus the four directional off-screen tests and their combination.

nodes.name: overlaps?
nodes.summary: The rectangle collision test games run every frame: two rectangles touch when on each axis neither starts past where the other ends. Touching edges count as a hit.

nodes.name: off_left?
nodes.summary: True once the rectangle is fully past the screen's left edge — its right side has crossed x = 0.

nodes.name: off_right?
nodes.summary: True once the rectangle is fully past the screen's right edge — its left side has reached the screen width.

nodes.name: above_top?
nodes.summary: True once the rectangle is fully past the top edge — the case a bullet flying off the top of the screen needs.

nodes.name: below_bottom?
nodes.summary: True once the rectangle is fully past the bottom edge — the case an enemy that should respawn after falling off the screen needs.

nodes.name: off_screen?
nodes.summary: True when the rectangle is fully past any edge, so nothing of it still shows. Composed from the four directional tests.

nodes.name: box.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the handle the `box` verb returns: a rectangle in screen space used for collision tests, which draws nothing itself. Each coordinate may be a fixed number, a variable or an expression, so one box can describe a moving thing as naturally as a fixed wall.

nodes.name: Box
nodes.summary: A collision rectangle built from a corner and a size. It mixes in Bounds for `overlaps?` and the screen-edge tests, and coerces every coordinate to an expression Value so its edges read back as live expressions.

nodes.name: branch.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the small handle returned by a condition's `.then` — the open `if` waiting for an optional `.else`. On its own it does nothing; calling `.else { }` fills in the block that runs when the condition was false.

nodes.name: Branch
nodes.summary: Holds the builder and the IR if-node a `.then` just recorded, so a following `.else` can attach its block to the same node.

nodes.name: else
nodes.summary: Records the statements to run when the condition was false. A missing block raises a friendly error naming the correct form rather than failing silently later.

nodes.name: debug.rb
nodes.summary: Debug-only build verbs that a test or measurement harness opts into with `extend`, deliberately kept out of the public game DSL. Its one hardware-only verb reads the live drawing scanline as a Value.
nodes.languageNotes: A Ruby module reopened inside Builder and mixed in only on request, so the verbs never reach a game developer even though they live on the same class.

nodes.name: Debug
nodes.summary: Opt-in mixin exposing read_scanline — the scanline the console is drawing right now, as a Value you can do arithmetic on — so a probe can measure how much of a frame's safe drawing window was used.

nodes.name: cli.rb
nodes.summary: The Thor-based `ruby-gba` command line: builds a declared game into a cartridge, inspects a ROM, scaffolds a starter game file, and reports the measured per-frame cost from the emulator.
nodes.languageNotes: Thor is required here and in bin/ruby-gba only — never by the library — so building a ROM in code or in a test carries no CLI dependency.

nodes.name: CLI
nodes.summary: Implements the build / inspect / new subcommands plus emulator-backed cost analysis, loading a game file that only declares its game and turning a guardrail failure into a plain-language message instead of a backtrace.

nodes.name: color.rb
nodes.summary: Console color handling: named presets plus rgb / rgb8 / from_hex constructors that validate channel ranges, and a resolver turning a color name or number into the raw 15-bit hardware value.
nodes.languageNotes: The console packs color into 15 bits as 0bBBBBBGGGGGRRRRR — five bits per channel, blue high and red low — so each channel runs 0-31, not 0-255.

nodes.name: Color
nodes.summary: Packs red/green/blue channels into the 15-bit color word and resolves named presets, raising a friendly error when 8-bit (0-255) values are passed where 0-31 are expected.

nodes.name: condition.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Condition, the yes/no test a comparison of two Values produces — the thing game code branches on with `.then` and an optional `.else`, and combines with `&` (both) or `|` (either).
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby cannot overload `&&`/`||`, so the single-character forms build a combined test. A Condition is also truthy to Ruby, so a native `if` would emit its body unconditionally at build time — which is why an unused Condition is tracked and reported.

nodes.name: Condition
nodes.summary: A runtime test: `.then` branches on it, `&`/`|` compose it, and an instance that is built but never branched on is caught and reported against the line the author actually wrote.

nodes.name: direction.rb
nodes.summary: The shared vocabulary of screen directions — four cardinal plus four diagonal names mapped to [dx, dy] unit steps — so anything that moves or faces a way says "move left" instead of doing coordinate arithmetic.

nodes.name: Direction
nodes.summary: Maps a direction name to its unit step in screen coordinates (up decreases y) and reports whether a name is known, raising a friendly error on a typo that would otherwise move nothing.

nodes.name: emulator.rb
nodes.summary: The single seam between the library and the emulator it verifies ROMs on. Every path that needs a real core — the Verifier, debug scripts, emulator-backed tests — goes through here, so the backend can be swapped in one place.
nodes.languageNotes: The backend is gemba-core, a headless libmgba probe vendored in-repo whose C extension must be built; load! raises loudly rather than letting verification silently skip.

nodes.name: Emulator
nodes.summary: Loads the emulator backend on first use (putting its in-repo lib on the load path), exposes the core class, and opens or probes a ROM file, with a clear actionable error when the extension is not built.

nodes.name: field_ref.rb
nodes.summary: Defines FieldRef, the mutable handle to one field of one pool instance at a runtime slot index — what a pool's `each` hands the game as `b.x`, `b.y`, and so on.

nodes.name: FieldRef
nodes.summary: A Value subclass that reads and writes an instance's slot in the field's backing list, so `b.y.add b.vy` reads like an ordinary variable while really meaning `y[i] = y[i] + vy[i]`.

nodes.name: font.rb
nodes.summary: The bitmap font model: glyphs stored as row-bytes plus the metrics to lay them out, with per-glyph widths, pixel walking for drawing, text measurement, and a glyph-art definition builder.
nodes.languageNotes: Each glyph row is one byte whose low bits are pixels (MSB leftmost). Height is fixed per font, but each glyph carries its own width, so a proportional font packs an 'i' tighter than an 'm'.

nodes.name: Font
nodes.summary: A named collection of glyphs with layout metrics: walks the set pixels of a string, measures text width by advancing per glyph, and counts lit pixels for the draw-cost model.

nodes.name: Font::Definition
nodes.summary: The glyph-art builder behind `font :name do glyph "A", ART end` — turns ASCII art rows into row-bytes and checks every glyph shares the font's height.

nodes.name: fonts.rb
nodes.summary: The registry of named fonts that `draw_text ..., font: :tiny` resolves through, so backends and the off-screen guardrail look a font up by name instead of reaching for one hardwired font.

nodes.name: Fonts
nodes.summary: Registers, looks up, and lists named Font objects and names the default, listing the fonts that do exist when an unknown name (almost always a typo) is asked for.

nodes.name: func_dumper.rb
nodes.summary: Disassembles named lowered functions out of a finished ROM and writes the listing to an injectable output stream — the machinery behind the `dump_func` debug verb.

nodes.name: FuncDumper
nodes.summary: Takes a ROM plus the byte spans the backend recorded per function and prints the machine code the lowering actually produced, resolving a bare scene name to its generated function.

nodes.name: game.rb
nodes.summary: Defines the Game handle that `RubyGBA.game` records without building anything, plus the registry the CLI reads — separating declaring a game from building it so the tool owns the output path and reporting.

nodes.name: Game
nodes.summary: A declared but unbuilt game: exposes #program (the op-tree the headless interpreter runs in tests) and #build_rom (the finished cartridge), plus a friendly default output filename derived from the title.

nodes.name: grid.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Grid, a board of equal-sized cells painted one at a time, so a tile-shaped game talks in cell coordinates and never multiplies by the cell size itself.
nodes.languageNotes: Painting only the cells that changed, instead of clearing and redrawing the whole board, is what keeps the picture from tearing — only a handful of writes fit in the brief safe drawing window each frame.

nodes.name: Grid
nodes.summary: Converts cell coordinates to pixels for set_cell / clear_cell (a cleared cell goes back to the background color) and raises friendly errors for an out-of-range cell, an odd cell size, or a board that overruns the screen.

nodes.name: hardware_sprite.rb
nodes.summary: Defines HardwareSprite, the handle to a moving picture the console composites over the background in tiled mode, presenting exactly the same surface as the software Sprite used in bitmap mode.
nodes.languageNotes: In tiled mode the console draws sprites on top of the background for free, so there is no draw call each frame and no trail to erase — unlike the save-under software sprite.

nodes.name: HardwareSprite
nodes.summary: A hardware sprite handle: x/y Values, directional and flipbook poses, wall-aware movement through blocked_by, clamping to the screen from its own size, and collision that is per-pixel by default.

nodes.name: inspector.rb
nodes.summary: Inspects and pretty-prints a ROM file: the cartridge header, whether its checksum is valid, and a disassembly of the code region — for debugging generated ROMs without reaching for a hex editor.

nodes.name: Inspector
nodes.summary: Reads a cartridge header (title, game and maker code, entry branch, fixed byte, checksum) and decodes ARM instructions — including rotated immediates, push/pop, and branches — into a readable listing.

nodes.name: instrument.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Instrument, a playable instrument built from one recorded sample: you play notes and chords on it, and the framework covers the whole keyboard from that single recording.
nodes.languageNotes: A higher or lower note is the same recording read faster or slower, shifted from the sample's own recorded pitch — so one .wav becomes a keyboard.

nodes.name: Instrument
nodes.summary: Plays one or several notes on a wrapped Sample, each note becoming a pitched voice in the mixer so a chord sounds together, and stops them all again.

nodes.name: list.rb
nodes.summary: Defines List, a bounded ordered collection whose length changes as the game runs — a snake's growing body, a queue of shots on screen — with methods that read like working with a Ruby array.

nodes.name: List
nodes.summary: The collection peer of Value: push / shift / pop / []= record statements into the program, while [], first, last, and length return Values that compose in expressions, and each walks the live entries.

nodes.name: music.rb
nodes.summary: Music sequencing: a build-time note/rest/tempo DSL that resolves a song into frame-and-frequency pairs every backend replays, with one line of notes or several parts layered as voices.
nodes.languageNotes: Durations become frame counts from the tempo, so the whole score is resolved at build time and a backend only has to play the right frequency on the right frame.

nodes.name: Music
nodes.summary: The music namespace: the note-name to frequency table, duration maths, and the contexts that turn a written score into a resolved sequence the backends share.

nodes.name: Music::VoiceContext
nodes.summary: Collects one part's notes and rests into timed events, resolving a pitch name (or raw Hz) to a frequency and a duration name to a frame count, and reports the part's total length.

nodes.name: Music::SongContext
nodes.summary: The `song do ... end` block context: sets tempo, forwards bare notes to a default voice, groups notes into named voices, and enforces the two-voice budget with a plain-language message.

nodes.name: pixel_bounds.rb
nodes.summary: Makes a sprite's overlaps? shape-accurate: on top of the plain box test, when both sides are per-pixel sprites it also checks whether their drawn pixels actually meet.
nodes.languageNotes: The cheap box overlap is a gate — pairs nowhere near each other fail it and never reach the per-pixel walk — so the accuracy costs nothing for the far-apart pairs that make up most of a frame.

nodes.name: PixelBounds
nodes.summary: Mixin that refines overlaps? into a per-pixel test for sprite-versus-sprite, falling back to the plain rectangle for a Box or a sprite pinned to an explicit hitbox.

nodes.name: pool.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Pool, a fixed-capacity set of component instances — bullets, enemies, particles, coins — so a game gets many of a behaving thing without hand-managing parallel lists that desync.
nodes.languageNotes: Each field is a backing list with an active column and a free stack of open slot indices, so spawn and remove are O(1), a live instance keeps a stable slot, and no field can be touched without the others.

nodes.name: Pool
nodes.summary: Drives the backing lists, active column, and free stack behind spawn / each / count / full?, including the recycle-oldest policy when the pool is full and optional auto-drawn sprites per live instance.

nodes.name: Pool::Instance
nodes.summary: The row handle `each` yields: named fields resolve through method_missing to mutable FieldRef Values, it can retire itself, and it carries a collision box from the pool's image for overlaps? and screen clamping.

nodes.name: rom.rb
nodes.summary: Manages the raw cartridge byte buffer and writes the header — logo, title, game and maker codes, fixed byte, checksum — then finalizes and pads the image to a power of two.
nodes.languageNotes: Every offset comes from the shared Constants rather than a magic number, which makes a header write mistake easy to spot; the console's BIOS refuses a cartridge whose header does not check out.

nodes.name: ROM
nodes.summary: Emits and patches machine code into a cartridge buffer, finalizes a validated header, can explain the source program's per-frame cost, and writes the finished image to disk.

nodes.name: rom_validator.rb
nodes.summary: Validates a finished cartridge image for the structural faults that make the BIOS or an accurate emulator reject it: too small, a wrong fixed byte or logo, a bad checksum, a misdirected entry branch, no code, an empty title.
nodes.languageNotes: These checks only make sense after lowering, once real bytes exist — unlike the IR guardrails, which reason about the program before any code is emitted.

nodes.name: ROMValidator
nodes.summary: Runs the post-lowering structural checks over a ROM buffer or file and reports errors (the ROM will not run) separately from warnings (it runs, but something is off).

nodes.name: sample.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Sample, the handle to a recorded clip played back through the sampled-audio hardware rather than synthesized as a tone on a PSG voice.
nodes.languageNotes: The framework manages the sound FIFO, the DMA that feeds it, and the timer that clocks the playback rate, so playing a real recording is just `boom.play`.

nodes.name: Sample
nodes.summary: Plays a recorded clip once, looping, at a chosen volume level, or pitch-shifted to another note, and validates a requested note against the known note table with a friendly error.

nodes.name: sound.rb
nodes.summary: The shared meaning of the sound ops in two layers: a hardware-free musical layer every backend agrees on, and a Registers layer that encodes those values into console sound-register writes.
nodes.languageNotes: Splitting musical meaning from register encoding is what lets a headless interpreter report "an 880 Hz blip played" with no notion of registers, while the ROM backend writes the real hardware bits.

nodes.name: Sound
nodes.summary: Resolves a beep's tone and overrides, a noise preset, or a wave shape into concrete musical values — frequency in Hz, duty, decay, volume — with no hardware detail involved.

nodes.name: Sound::Registers
nodes.summary: Encodes resolved musical values into the console's sound-register writes: the two square channels for effects and music notes, the noise channel for percussion, and the wave channel with its packed wavetable.

nodes.name: sprite.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Sprite, the software sprite handle for bitmap mode: a named image with a position it owns, that moves around the screen leaving no trail behind it.
nodes.languageNotes: Bitmap mode has no sprite hardware, so the sprite saves the pixels underneath itself before drawing and paints them back before drawing at the new spot — the save-under trick a plain blit cannot do.

nodes.name: Sprite
nodes.summary: A software sprite handle: x/y Values, facing and flipbook poses, move / move_to / clamp_to_screen, hide and show, and per-pixel collision, recording erase-then-draw for every frame.

nodes.name: table.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Table, a read-only array shipped as ROM data at build time and read at run time by a Value index — how a game precomputes a sine or distance table the console cannot afford each frame.
nodes.languageNotes: An out-of-range index is made safe by the read itself: a power-of-two table wraps it (what an angle wants), any other size clamps it to the ends.

nodes.name: Table
nodes.summary: Indexes a build-time constant table with a Value, Integer, or variable name and returns a Value that composes in expressions; its length is a plain build-time Integer.

nodes.name: test_patterns.rb
nodes.summary: Built-in diagnostic ROM generators producing unmistakable pictures — solid fill, color bars, corners, crosshair — for checking that the emulator setup and rendering path work at all.

nodes.name: TestPatterns
nodes.summary: Builds small self-contained ROMs whose output is obvious on screen, so a blank result points at the emulator setup rather than the user's own code.

nodes.name: timer.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Timer, the handle to a hardware counter that runs at a chosen rate independent of the frame loop — for timed work and, later, for clocking sampled audio.
nodes.languageNotes: The requested rate becomes a prescaler and reload value behind the scenes, and `ticks` counts how many times the counter has overflowed since it started, wrapping at 65536.

nodes.name: Timer
nodes.summary: Exposes the tick count as a Value that reads and compares like any other, runs a body precisely on every tick off the timer's interrupt, and stops the counter.

nodes.name: value.rb
nodes.summary: Defines Value, the central handle to a variable, a literal, or an arithmetic expression over them — the object ordinary Ruby operators build bigger expressions from.
nodes.languageNotes: Comparisons and arithmetic only build bigger nodes, so nothing is committed to the program until a Condition branches or a mutator runs; mutating an expression Value, which names no variable, is a friendly error.

nodes.name: Value
nodes.summary: Wraps a value node: arithmetic operators build larger expressions, comparison operators return a Condition instead of a Ruby boolean, and set / add / sub / clamp / approach / abs / flip record statements against the named variable.

nodes.name: verifier.rb
nodes.summary: Loads a ROM in the emulator and reads back the pixels it actually rendered, plus memory, variables, and audio energy — the definitive answer to "did my ROM draw anything?" without squinting at a window.

nodes.name: Verifier
nodes.summary: Runs a ROM for a number of frames with optional key input, then answers pixel, region, memory, variable, and audio queries, plus a printable character map and report of what was drawn.

nodes.name: version.rb
nodes.summary: Declares the library's version constant, kept in its own file so tooling and the gemspec can read it without loading the rest of the library.

nodes.name: wav.rb
nodes.summary: Loads a .wav file into the 8-bit signed mono PCM the sampled-audio hardware plays, converting whatever the file holds — 8- or 16-bit, mono or stereo — while keeping its own sample rate.
nodes.languageNotes: A WAV is a RIFF container of chunks shaped [4-byte id][4-byte little-endian size][payload], each padded to an even length, so a reader skips past any chunk it does not want.

nodes.name: Wav
nodes.summary: Finds and parses a WAV's fmt and data chunks and converts the samples down to one channel of signed 8-bit PCM, raising a friendly error for a compressed or float file.

nodes.name: calibrate_cost_model.rb
nodes.summary: Calibrates the cost model's per-op weights against the real emulator and writes the result as a source-controlled Ruby fixture the cost model loads — no hand-copying and no JSON or YAML.
nodes.languageNotes: Differencing two ROMs that differ only in the op under test cancels the fixed per-frame overhead, so what remains is that op's own cost measured in scanlines.

nodes.name: stable_busy
nodes.summary: Builds a ROM whose per-frame loop repeats the op under test a known number of times and measures it, retrying until the reading settles.

nodes.name: measure
nodes.summary: Runs a built ROM on the emulator and reads back the CPU scanlines its frame actually burns.

nodes.name: mixer_busy
nodes.summary: Measures the per-frame cost of the sampled-audio mixer with a given number of voices sounding at once.

nodes.name: music_busy
nodes.summary: Measures the per-frame cost of music playback for a given number of layered voices.

nodes.name: cost_model.rb
nodes.summary: Estimates how much work an IR program does per frame — drawing, sound and logic — measured in scanlines, so the framework can warn before the ROM ever runs that a game will tear or drop below 60fps. It is the engine behind the draw-budget guardrails and the user-facing `rom.explain` report.
nodes.languageNotes: Costs are expressed in scanlines because the console draws one scanline at a time; the vertical blank (the safe window to change the screen) is about 68 of the frame's 228 scanlines, so a single number reads directly as a fraction of the safe window.

nodes.name: CostModel
nodes.summary: Walks an IR tree and prices every op against calibrated per-op weights, rolling the result into a cost tree split across drawing, sound and logic. It models the shape of the work — a repeat multiplies its body, a list-driven loop counts to capacity, a scene dispatch costs its heaviest branch — and flags any op kind it does not know how to price rather than silently counting it as free.

nodes.name: analyze
nodes.summary: Returns one frame's work as a structured cost tree of { op, label, cost, children } — the game loop's body when there is one, otherwise the one-time boot draws of a static program.

nodes.name: build
nodes.summary: Recursively converts one IR node into a cost-tree node, dispatching control-flow kinds (case, call, repeat, timer) to their own builders so a container's cost aggregates its children correctly.

nodes.name: op_cost
nodes.summary: Prices a single leaf op in scanlines from the weight table — DMA rows, plotted pixels, sound register writes — and records any unrecognized kind as unpriced so a newly added op cannot slip through counted as free.

nodes.name: budget_thresholds
nodes.summary: Parametric analysis that solves for the tip-over item count: how large a per-frame-redrawn list can grow before the frame goes over budget, reported only when that count is reachable within the list's declared capacity.

nodes.name: scene_verdicts
nodes.summary: Judges each scene against its own display mode's budget, so a heavy direct-color scene is still caught in a game whose other scenes are double-buffered and would otherwise widen the whole-program budget.

nodes.name: render
nodes.summary: Renders the human-readable per-frame cost breakdown behind `rom.explain` — the category tree, hottest ops and budget summary — writing every line through a Printer so color is decided in one place.

nodes.name: as_json
nodes.summary: Dumps the cost analysis as structured JSON — the machine-readable twin of the rendered report, used by tests to assert on the estimate.

nodes.name: measured_weights.rb
nodes.summary: Generated table of empirically calibrated per-op costs in scanlines, measured on real hardware through gemba-core by tools/calibrate_cost_model.rb. These measured values override the cost model's hand estimates.
nodes.languageNotes: A generated fixture kept as a plain frozen Hash constant, so re-calibration is a committed diff rather than a runtime measurement.

nodes.name: printer.rb
nodes.summary: Output layer for the cost estimate: the cost model hands each line its meaning (how hot it is, whether it is a group heading) and a Printer decides how to show it — plain text to a file or pipe, an ANSI green-to-red heatmap to a terminal.

nodes.name: Printer
nodes.summary: Base printer holding the shared row layout and the heat severity scale, plus the factory that picks a plain or color printer — tinting only for an interactive terminal with NO_COLOR unset, so a captured or piped report stays plain automatically.

nodes.name: PlainPrinter
nodes.summary: Writes every line verbatim, ignoring severity and emphasis, so a captured or piped report is byte-for-byte identical to the output from before colors existed.

nodes.name: ColorPrinter
nodes.summary: Wraps each line in ANSI codes: a green-to-red tint by how much of the frame budget it uses, with group headings bold and underlined under only their label so no rule runs across to the value column.

nodes.name: guardrails.rb
nodes.summary: The guardrail mechanism: a registry of checks plus the validation pass that runs them over the IR before lowering, defining the Finding and Fix value objects, the Report, and the always-on BUILTIN_CHECKS list. Individual hardware knowledge lives in the Checks under guardrails/, not here.
nodes.languageNotes: Checks are duck-typed — anything with #detect(program) -> [Finding] qualifies — so an effect pack or a single game can register its own footgun check alongside the frozen builtins.

nodes.name: Guardrails
nodes.summary: Namespace and registry for the validation checks: holds the registered extension checks, composes them with the frozen builtins into the default set read fresh each pass, and can be cleared back to builtins only.

nodes.name: Finding
nodes.summary: One problem a guardrail found: its severity (error breaks the ROM, warning is advisory), a plain-language message written for the person, an optional safe Fix, and the DSL call site. The '(at file:line)' suffix is appended in one place so every check gets it for free.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby Data.define with a custom initialize supplying keyword defaults — an immutable value object rather than a Struct.

nodes.name: Report
nodes.summary: The result of a validation pass — the possibly auto-fixed program plus every finding — so a caller can split errors from warnings, raise on real problems, or emit the plain-language messages to an injectable stream.

nodes.name: Validator
nodes.summary: The validation pass itself: runs each check over the IR tree in order and, when a check offers a safe fix, applies it, threads the corrected program into the checks that follow, and downgrades that finding from an error to a warning.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Executes every check against the program, applying and recording auto-fixes as warnings when autofix is on, and returns a Report carrying the resulting program and all findings.

nodes.name: frame_reach.rb
nodes.summary: Shared frame-path analysis for the per-frame guardrails: answers 'what does this game loop actually run every frame?' once instead of in each check.

nodes.name: FrameReach
nodes.summary: Collects the statements reachable every frame from a game loop, following call and case dispatch into funcs but deliberately stopping at a body guarded by a `pressed` edge — that fires on a press, not steadily, so a board painted once on START is correctly excluded from the steady path.

nodes.name: per_frame_scope.rb
nodes.summary: Shared machinery for the one-time-setup guardrails, which all have the same shape: a verb meant to run once written directly inside a per-frame context, where it silently re-runs every frame.

nodes.name: PerFrameScope
nodes.summary: Identifies which containers re-run every frame — the game loop, a repeat, an every() timer, or a func reached by unconditional calls from one — and names them in plain language for the message. A call behind a condition or input edge is excluded, which is what keeps a one-off reset routine from being mistaken for per-frame setup.

nodes.name: screen_mode_set.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the classic silent-black-screen footgun: a program that draws but never picks a screen mode, so the whole game runs invisibly with no crash to point at it.

nodes.name: ScreenModeSet
nodes.summary: Fires when the program contains a drawing op yet no `screen` op anywhere. Because nothing appears on the console until a mode is chosen, and the fix is completely safe, it auto-prepends `screen :bitmap` ahead of every statement and downgrades itself to a warning.

nodes.name: vblank_sync.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a game loop that never waits for the screen to refresh, so it spins thousands of times a second instead of 60 — the 'my game runs way too fast / it flickers' report.

nodes.name: VblankSync
nodes.summary: Warns for every loop from which no frame sync is reachable, following call and case dispatch into funcs because a game may sync inside a dispatched scene rather than in the loop body. A reachable raw block counts as synced, since it is opaque and staying quiet beats crying wolf.

nodes.name: termination.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a program whose top-level flow just ends: with no `halt` and no forever-running game loop the console keeps executing whatever bytes follow in memory, which is garbage.

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.summary: Reads termination exactly off the IR where scanning finished machine code was only a heuristic: top-level statements run unconditionally in order, so the program stops if and only if one never returns — a halt, an always-infinite loop, or a call into a func that itself never returns. Definitions are skipped since they emit nothing in line.

nodes.name: off_screen_draw.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a draw whose whole footprint lands outside the 240x160 screen — the 'why is my sprite missing' mystery, a safe no-op with no crash to point at it.

nodes.name: OffScreenDraw
nodes.summary: Computes build-time-constant bounds for each positioned draw — pixels, rects, text, digits and blits sized from their embedded bitmap — and warns when the footprint misses the screen entirely, naming the coordinates and suggesting a swapped x and y. A partly off-screen draw is intentional and stays silent, and a draw at a runtime position is left to the safe clipping at run time.

nodes.name: orphaned_condition.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the native-`if` slip: a DSL comparison is a Condition object and Ruby treats any object as true, so `if x > 5` runs its body every time with the comparison silently ignored.

nodes.name: OrphanedCondition
nodes.summary: The one check that cannot detect by walking the IR — an unused Condition never records a node — so it is constructed with the builder's leftover pending Conditions and turns each into an error, telling the user to write `(x > 5).then { }` instead of `if x > 5`. It ignores the program entirely, which lets it still run as an ordinary check in the Validator's list.

nodes.name: draw_budget.rb
nodes.summary: Cost-model-driven guardrail for the tearing footgun: a game that draws more each frame than fits the brief safe window spills into the visible frame, so the picture tears and it gets worse as the game grows.

nodes.name: DrawBudget
nodes.summary: Estimates the steady per-frame cost through the CostModel and warns when it exceeds the budget, phrasing the message by mode: single-buffered over-budget means tearing, double-buffered means a frame rate below 60fps. A game that switches modes between scenes is judged scene by scene so a heavy direct-color scene is not hidden by a buffered one.

nodes.name: budget_threshold.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a growing collection drawn item by item every frame — a snake's body, a swarm of bullets — which looks fine while small and only starts to tear once it grows, a baffling bug to hit late.

nodes.name: BudgetThreshold
nodes.summary: Where the draw-budget check says 'this frame draws too much', this one leans on the cost model's parametric analysis to say how big the collection can get before it does — the tip-over item count — and points at the list to cap. It only speaks when that count is reachable within the list's declared capacity.

nodes.name: channel_conflict.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a sound-voice collision: a two-part song needs a second voice, and the only one left is the same one `beep` plays on, so the two keep cutting each other off — silent and baffling if you do not know the console has only a few voices.

nodes.name: ChannelConflict
nodes.summary: Fires only when the program both beeps and plays a song with two or more voices, warning once per such song. Advisory, since the two really can share the voice if the user does not mind them interrupting each other.

nodes.name: redraw_everything.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the high-signal shape of the tearing footgun: a game loop that clears the whole screen every frame and also repaints a collection that grows as the game runs, so the redraw gets heavier until the picture tears.

nodes.name: RedrawEverything
nodes.summary: The cheap structural companion to the cost estimator — no weights, just the pattern of a full-screen clear plus a repeat over a list's length whose body paints — so it has near-zero false positives. It looks only at the steady per-frame path and stays silent when the program double-buffers, since buffering is the cure for exactly this footgun.

nodes.name: sprite_cleared_each_frame.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the sprite-that-gets-wiped footgun: a loop that moves a sprite and also clears the whole screen every frame, so the clear erases the field the sprite just restored and the sprite flickers or vanishes.

nodes.name: SpriteClearedEachFrame
nodes.summary: Recognizes a sprite structurally by the save-region and restore-region ops nothing else emits, then warns when the steady per-frame path also contains a clear_screen or a display-sized fill. A clear behind a `pressed` edge is a transition, not steady work, and is correctly left alone.

nodes.name: manual_sprite_blit.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the double-drawn-sprite footgun: hand-blitting an image that is already a sprite stamps a second copy nothing ever erases, so it smears the very trail the sprite was chosen to avoid.

nodes.name: ManualSpriteBlit
nodes.summary: Classifies blits with no build-time bookkeeping: a blit sitting beside a save- or restore-region op is one of the framework's own sprite draws, so any other blit of the same image is one the developer wrote by hand and gets the warning.

nodes.name: seed_in_loop.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for a one-time-setup footgun: `seed` written inside a per-frame context keeps resetting the random stream to the same point, so every random value comes back identical and the game feels eerily fixed, with no crash to explain it.

nodes.name: SeedInLoop
nodes.summary: Tells a re-seed from a churn on the tree: a seed assigns the stream's state without reading it, while roll/rand/randomize advance it by referencing it. Only an unconditional seed directly inside a per-frame body is flagged, so a deliberate re-seed behind an input edge proceeds untouched.

nodes.name: list_in_loop.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for the sibling one-time-setup footgun: a `list` declared inside a per-frame context is re-created empty every frame, so anything pushed onto it is thrown away and the collection mysteriously refuses to fill.

nodes.name: ListInLoop
nodes.summary: Flags only an unconditional list_new that is a direct statement of a per-frame body, so a list created inside a condition (a deliberate reset) is left alone, and reading or changing a list in the loop is untouched.

nodes.name: iwram_budget.rb
nodes.summary: Guardrail for silently overrunning the console's 32KB of fast on-chip RAM: the allocator never looks at the ceiling, so a program that reserves too much corrupts whatever memory follows and produces a black-screen ROM with nothing to say why.

nodes.name: IwramBudget
nodes.summary: Sums everything the whole program reserves — a word per variable, a list's slots plus two bookkeeping words, a moving sprite's save-under buffer — against the usable budget after the call stack's headroom, and stops the build with a plain-language error naming the total and the biggest users. A pool's several backing lists collapse into one contributor, since the author declared one pool, not five lists.
nodes.languageNotes: Fast on-chip RAM (IWRAM) is 32KB total, and this reserves 4KB of headroom for the call stack and framework scratch, so the program's data budget is 28KB.

nodes.name: builder.rb
nodes.summary: The core `Builder` class: the DSL context a `RubyGBA.build` block is evaluated in. It mixes in all seventeen verb concerns so the DSL surface stays flat, owns the machinery every concern shares (variable allocation, deferred func bodies, sprite/HUD registries, boot-time initialization), and grows the IR op-tree a backend later lowers to a ROM.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby mixin composition: each file under builder/ is a module included into Builder, so every verb stays a plain top-level method inside the build block.

nodes.name: Builder
nodes.summary: The DSL context itself. It includes every verb concern, allocates variables in fast RAM on first mention, defers func bodies until finalize (so a call may name a function defined later), tracks the live sprite, HUD and animation registries, and pushes each recorded statement onto the container stack that shapes the IR tree.

nodes.name: EntryContext
nodes.summary: The small context the `entry` escape hatch runs in, exposing raw instruction helpers such as `loop_forever` and `nop` for what the DSL cannot express.

nodes.name: list
nodes.summary: Declares a named, bounded list whose length changes as the game runs (a snake's body, a queue of shots) and returns a handle to push, pop, index and iterate it. Capacity is rounded up to a power of two so an index wraps cheaply and every backend overflows at the same point.

nodes.name: table
nodes.summary: Declares a build-time Ruby array shipped as read-only ROM data and read at run time by a Value index — a precomputed sine or distance table. Values are checked to fit the chosen element width, and an out-of-range index wraps or clamps instead of reading garbage.

nodes.name: entry
nodes.summary: The raw escape hatch: runs a block in an EntryContext so a program can emit instructions the DSL cannot express.

nodes.name: emit_pending_functions
nodes.summary: The finalize step that evaluates every deferred `func` and `scene` body after the main block has run — which is what lets a `call` refer to a function defined later — then verifies that every call and case target actually exists.

nodes.name: ensure_var
nodes.summary: Allocates a variable in fast RAM the first time it is mentioned and records its address, so any verb can name a variable without the program declaring it up front.

nodes.name: resolve_asset_path
nodes.summary: Resolves an asset path (an image, a WAV, a CSV map) relative to the user's own script rather than the process working directory, so an example runs the same from any directory.

nodes.name: collision.rb
nodes.summary: Gives the DSL the `box` verb — a rectangle built from a top-left corner and a size that draws nothing and exists only to be collision-tested. The `overlaps?` test itself lives on the shape, so a sprite, which already knows its own bounds, needs no box at all.

nodes.name: Collision
nodes.summary: The collision concern mixed into Builder: one verb that makes a testable rectangle, with the overlap test deliberately living on the shape instead of here.

nodes.name: box
nodes.summary: Makes a rectangle from a top-left corner and a size for collision tests. Each coordinate may be a fixed number, a variable, or an expression, so one box can follow a moving ball while another pins a fixed wall.

nodes.name: composition.rb
nodes.summary: Gives the DSL the `pool` verb: declare a component's named fields plus a capacity and get a handle that spawns, iterates and retires live instances. A pool desugars entirely onto lists, an active column and a repeat, so its fields can never fall out of step and every backend runs it unchanged.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.summary: The composition concern: the `pool` verb plus the validation and boot-time storage setup behind it, including the reserved field names, the spawn-when-full policies, and the fast-RAM ceiling that turns an impossible capacity into a friendly build error.

nodes.name: pool
nodes.summary: Declares a pool of a component — named fields with defaults plus a capacity — and returns a handle that spawns, iterates and retires live instances. Give it an `image:` and every live instance draws itself as a hardware sprite with its own collision box.

nodes.name: validate_pool!
nodes.summary: Rejects a bad pool declaration with a plain-language build error: a name that is not a Symbol, a non-positive capacity, a field name that would shadow a Pool method, or a pool too large for fast RAM.

nodes.name: setup_pool_storage
nodes.summary: Builds the pool's storage once at boot — one list per field plus the active column and the free-slot stack — so the parallel columns can never desync.

nodes.name: control_flow.rb
nodes.summary: The control-flow verbs a game's shape is written with: `game_loop`, `wait_vblank`, `repeat`, the timed triggers `every` and `after`, `halt`/`debug_halt`, and the low-level `if_eq`/`if_gt` comparison family. `wait_vblank` is also where the framework repaints sprites and steps flipbook animations, which is why a sprite never needs a draw call.
nodes.languageNotes: The if_eq through if_le family is generated with define_method over a condition table rather than written out one method at a time.

nodes.name: ControlFlow
nodes.summary: The control-flow concern: the loop and timing verbs, the stop verbs, the generated comparison verbs, and the per-frame repaint and animation stepping that hang off wait_vblank.

nodes.name: wait_vblank
nodes.summary: Waits for the one safe window each frame to change the screen, then repaints everything: erase all software sprites, draw them all back, present the hardware sprites and HUD glyphs, and step each flipbook animation. Erasing every sprite before drawing any is what stops overlapping sprites from smearing copies of each other.

nodes.name: game_loop
nodes.summary: Wraps a block as the per-frame loop: its statements become the loop body in the IR tree and the backend adds the jump back to the top.

nodes.name: repeat
nodes.summary: Runs a block a number of times counted at run time, handing the body a Value for the current index — the counterpart to Ruby's `times` for when the count is only decided while the game runs.

nodes.name: every
nodes.summary: Runs a block on a repeating beat given in frames or seconds, with the counter allocated, cleared at boot and managed for the user. The interval stays first-class in the IR so the cost model can read it directly.

nodes.name: after
nodes.summary: Runs a block exactly once, a number of frames or seconds from now — a one-shot delay whose hidden counter stops as soon as it reaches its target.

nodes.name: debug_halt
nodes.summary: A bisecting breakpoint: stops the build here so nothing written after it reaches the ROM, and warns so the call is not left behind by accident.

nodes.name: drawing.rb
nodes.summary: The bitmap drawing verbs: `screen` picks the display (including the tear-free double-buffered bitmap), then `pixel`, `fill_rect`, `dma_fill_rect`, `clear_screen`, `draw_rect_at` and `grid` put color on it. Remembering the chosen mode is what later lets `sprite` decide between a software and a hardware sprite.

nodes.name: Drawing
nodes.summary: The drawing concern: the friendly screen-mode presets that stand in for raw display-register values, and the verbs that paint pixels, rectangles and whole screens.

nodes.name: screen
nodes.summary: Picks the display — a direct-color bitmap, a tiled layer screen, or an affine one — validating the name and the tear-free option, and remembers the chosen mode so `sprite` can later pick software or hardware sprites.

nodes.name: pixel
nodes.summary: Draws a single pixel at a fixed coordinate, after checking the coordinate is on screen.

nodes.name: fill_rect
nodes.summary: Draws a filled rectangle at a fixed position and size.

nodes.name: clear_screen
nodes.summary: Paints the whole screen one color in a single block transfer.

nodes.name: dma_fill_rect
nodes.summary: Fills a rectangle with the console's block-transfer hardware, the fast path for large fixed rectangles.

nodes.name: draw_rect_at
nodes.summary: Draws a fixed-size rectangle at a position decided while the game runs, so a variable can move it around the screen.

nodes.name: grid
nodes.summary: Lays out a board of equal cells and returns a handle that paints them by cell coordinate, so a tile game reads in cells instead of pixel arithmetic.

nodes.name: images.rb
nodes.summary: The image and color verbs: `image` defines a bitmap from ASCII art, a raw pixel array, or an image file; `blit` draws one at a runtime position; `rgb`, `rgb8` and `color` build 15-bit colors. It also records each image's visible-pixel bounds, which later becomes a sprite's default collision box.
nodes.languageNotes: Transparency is marked with the unused sixteenth bit of a BGR555 color (0x8000), a value a real color can never take.

nodes.name: Images
nodes.summary: The image concern: the three authoring forms `image` accepts, the blit verb, the color constructors, and the bookkeeping that remembers each image's size and visible bounds for the sprite and collision layers.

nodes.name: image
nodes.summary: Defines a named bitmap three ways — ASCII art with a character-to-color map, a raw pixel array, or an imported image file — and embeds it in the ROM for `blit`, `sprite` and `tiles` to use by name.

nodes.name: blit
nodes.summary: Draws a defined bitmap at a position that may be a variable, clipping at the screen edges.

nodes.name: define_ascii_image
nodes.summary: Turns a block of ASCII art plus a character-to-color map into a bitmap, taking the dimensions from the art's own shape and honoring a character mapped to `:transparent`.

nodes.name: define_pixel_image
nodes.summary: Records a bitmap from raw width, height and pixel data, packs it to 15-bit color, and remembers its size and visible bounds for anything built on it.

nodes.name: input.rb
nodes.summary: The input verbs: `held` and `pressed` turn a button into a Condition you branch on with `.then` and compose with `&`/`|`, while `if_held` and `if_pressed` are the block forms. Button names are checked against the shared IR vocabulary, and a block passed to `held`/`pressed` raises a friendly error naming the dropped `.then`.

nodes.name: Input
nodes.summary: The input concern: four button verbs plus the two guardrails that make a mistyped button name and a dropped `.then` into plain-language errors instead of silent no-ops.

nodes.name: if_held
nodes.summary: Runs a block only while a button is held down.

nodes.name: if_pressed
nodes.summary: Runs a block on the frame a button is first pressed — down now, up the frame before.

nodes.name: held
nodes.summary: Turns a button into a Condition that holds while it is down, for `.then` branching and `&`/`|` composition.

nodes.name: pressed
nodes.summary: Turns a button into a Condition true only on the frame it is first pressed.

nodes.name: music.rb
nodes.summary: The music verbs `song`, `play_song` and `stop_music`. A `song` block is evaluated in the note and tempo notation to produce a resolved score — each voice's frame-and-frequency pairs plus the song's length — which is recorded into the IR so every backend replays the same tune; music uses its own voice so it never clashes with beeps.

nodes.name: Music
nodes.summary: The music concern mixed into Builder. It is deliberately distinct from RubyGBA::Music, the note and tempo notation a `song` block is written in.

nodes.name: song
nodes.summary: Defines a named tune: evaluates the block in the note and tempo notation and records the resolved score, so a backend replays music from data rather than re-interpreting the DSL.

nodes.name: play_song
nodes.summary: Advances a defined song by one frame; call it once per frame inside the game loop. It refuses plainly if sound was never enabled or the song does not exist.

nodes.name: stop_music
nodes.summary: Silences the music voices, for a scene that should play no music.

nodes.name: randomness.rb
nodes.summary: The randomness verbs `seed`, `randomize`, `roll`, `rand` and `chance`, all built on one hidden multiply-and-add stream. The same seed always replays the same sequence on every backend, so a game is reproducible by default and opts in to unpredictability by stirring the stream while it waits for the player.
nodes.languageNotes: A draw reads the top sixteen bits of the state, because the low bits of a linear-congruential stream fall into a short and visible rhythm.

nodes.name: Randomness
nodes.summary: The randomness concern: the hidden stream variable, the multiply-and-add churn pinned so every backend agrees to the bit, and the five verbs that draw from it.

nodes.name: seed
nodes.summary: Sets the random stream's starting point. The same seed replays the same sequence every time, so a game can be made deterministic or seeded from something the player influences.

nodes.name: randomize
nodes.summary: Stirs the stream by one step. Called every frame while waiting for the player, it turns their reaction time into the game's only real source of unpredictability.

nodes.name: roll
nodes.summary: Draws a random whole number from an ordinary Ruby range into a named variable, folding the stream's high bits down into that range.

nodes.name: rand
nodes.summary: Draws a random number from a range into a hidden variable and hands back a Value, so two draws in one expression stay independent.

nodes.name: chance
nodes.summary: Returns a Condition true a given percent of the time, so a drop rate or a random event reads as a probability instead of a comparison against a raw draw.

nodes.name: sampled_audio.rb
nodes.summary: The sampled-audio verbs `sample` and `instrument`: define a recorded 8-bit PCM clip from a `.wav` file or from raw samples and get a handle that plays, loops, pitches and stops it. `instrument` wraps the same recording so one clip covers a whole keyboard of notes.

nodes.name: SampledAudio
nodes.summary: The sampled-audio concern: two verbs plus the loading and packing that turn a WAV file or a raw sample array into the PCM bytes the IR carries.

nodes.name: sample
nodes.summary: Defines a named 8-bit PCM sample from a WAV file or raw samples and returns a handle to play and stop it, rejecting an empty clip or a non-positive rate with a plain error.

nodes.name: instrument
nodes.summary: Wraps a sample as an instrument so one recording can be played as any note or as a chord.

nodes.name: sample_data
nodes.summary: Resolves a sample's bytes and rate from whichever source was given — a WAV file with its own rate, or raw pcm samples — insisting on exactly one of the two.

nodes.name: scenes.rb
nodes.summary: The subroutine and scene verbs: `func` and `call` for named routines whose bodies are deferred so definition order does not matter, `scene` for a named game state, `case_var` to run exactly one scene per frame from a state variable, and `dump_func` for a disassembly dump.

nodes.name: Scenes
nodes.summary: The scene and subroutine concern: the verbs that feed the builder's finalize step, which emits deferred bodies and verifies every call and case target resolves.

nodes.name: CaseContext
nodes.summary: The small collector a `case_var` block is evaluated in, gathering each `when_val` clause that maps a state value to a scene.

nodes.name: func
nodes.summary: Defines a named subroutine, storing the block to be evaluated after the main build block so definition order does not matter.

nodes.name: call
nodes.summary: Calls a named subroutine. The target is resolved by name when the tree is lowered, so it may be defined before or after the call.

nodes.name: scene
nodes.summary: Defines a named game state as a routine run once per frame while that state is active — internally a func under a reserved prefix, so a scene name can never clash with a function name.

nodes.name: case_var
nodes.summary: Dispatches to exactly one scene per frame based on a state variable's value, collecting the `when_val` clauses from the block and recording a single case node over them.

nodes.name: dump_func
nodes.summary: Queues a function or scene to be disassembled from the built ROM, for debugging.

nodes.name: sound.rb
nodes.summary: The sound-effect verbs: `enable_sound` turns the audio hardware on, `define_sound` names a reusable preset, and `beep`, `noise` and `wave` fire effects on the square, noise and wave voices. Every trigger checks that sound was enabled first and says so plainly if it was not, instead of playing silence.

nodes.name: Sound
nodes.summary: The sound-effect concern: the enable flag it shares with the music concern, the named presets, and the three voices a game fires effects on.

nodes.name: enable_sound
nodes.summary: Turns the audio hardware on, once. Without it every sound verb refuses rather than playing silently.

nodes.name: define_sound
nodes.summary: Names a reusable sound preset — frequency, wave shape, fade speed and volume — that `beep` can then fire by name.

nodes.name: beep
nodes.summary: Fires a one-off tone on the square-wave effects voice, from a preset name or a raw frequency.

nodes.name: noise
nodes.summary: Plays a percussion or explosion hit on the noise voice, from a preset like `:kick` or `:explosion`, or from pitch, decay and volume directly.

nodes.name: wave
nodes.summary: Plays a sustained tone with a chosen timbre — sine, triangle, sawtooth or square — on the wave voice, holding until it is stopped or replaced.

nodes.name: sprite_import.rb
nodes.summary: Adapters that read sprite art from files and tools into the poses the `sprite` verb consumes: slicing a sprite sheet into animation frames, slicing a directional sheet into per-direction poses, and importing a native Aseprite file with its layers, frame durations and named animations.

nodes.name: SpriteImport
nodes.summary: The sprite-art import concern: entirely private adapters, so the file adds no verbs of its own and only widens where `sprite` can get its pictures from.

nodes.name: import_frames
nodes.summary: Slices a sprite sheet into equal cells, defines each as an image in row-major order, and returns the frame names ready for the flipbook path — so importing frames needs no naming or numbering.

nodes.name: import_facing
nodes.summary: Slices a directional sprite sheet into `facing:` poses, reading each row as a direction and its columns as that direction's frames, so one file yields either a still pose per direction or a walk cycle each way.

nodes.name: import_aseprite
nodes.summary: Imports a sprite the way an artist authored it: reads the native Aseprite file or a JSON export, composites its layers, resolves frame durations, and exposes each named animation tag as a clip the sprite can play on demand.

nodes.name: sprites.rb
nodes.summary: The `sprite` verb and everything behind it: software save-under sprites on a bitmap screen, hardware sprites on a tiled screen, `facing:` poses, flipbook and per-direction animation, named Aseprite clips, and hitbox resolution. The handle is identical either way, so game code does not change when the screen mode does.

nodes.name: Sprites
nodes.summary: The sprite concern: one public verb over two lowering paths (software and hardware), four pose sources that are mutually exclusive by design, and the validation that turns a contradictory sprite declaration into a plain build error.

nodes.name: sprite
nodes.summary: The `sprite` verb: makes a named picture that moves around leaving no trail, choosing a software or a hardware sprite from the current screen mode and accepting exactly one pose source — `facing:` poses, a frame list, a sliced sheet, or an Aseprite file.

nodes.name: hardware_sprite
nodes.summary: Builds a tiled-mode sprite the console composites in hardware: reserves its name, boots its position and visibility, resolves its poses and hitbox, and registers it as an object drawn each frame. The handle mirrors a software sprite's so game code reads the same either way.

nodes.name: collision_box
nodes.summary: Resolves a sprite's collision box from its `hitbox:` option — the whole image, an inset on every side, an explicit rectangle, or the default box that hugs the visible pixels.

nodes.name: resolve_sprite_art
nodes.summary: Works out a sprite's poses, directions and pixel size from whichever art source it was given, so the software and hardware paths downstream see one uniform description.

nodes.name: resolve_directional_frames
