nodes.summary: Expands a `facing:` map whose directions each carry a list of frames into a per-direction animation, checking that every direction has the same number of frames.

nodes.name: validate_animation!
nodes.summary: Rejects contradictory or incomplete animation options with a plain-language build error — two pose sources at once, frames without a rate, or a rate with nothing to cycle.

nodes.name: clip_sprite
nodes.summary: Builds a software sprite driven by named animation clips imported from Aseprite, wiring the pose variable, the per-frame durations, and the clip a `play` call selects.

nodes.name: clip_hardware_sprite
nodes.summary: The hardware counterpart of clip_sprite: a tiled-mode sprite whose named clips the console composites, sharing the same handle so `play(:walk)` reads identically in either screen mode.

nodes.name: text.rb
nodes.summary: The on-screen writing verbs: `draw_text` for fixed words, `draw_number` for a live counter that follows its variable, and `font` for defining a font from glyph art. On a bitmap screen the glyphs are painted into the framebuffer; on a tiled screen each character becomes a small hardware-sprite glyph the console composites over the game.

nodes.name: Text
nodes.summary: The text concern: two verbs kept separate because a game uses words and numbers differently, each with a bitmap path and a tiled-HUD path, plus the glyph image cache both share.

nodes.name: font
nodes.summary: Defines a font from little glyph bitmaps, the way `image` defines art from ASCII, and registers it under a name `draw_text` can select. Glyphs share a height but may differ in width, so text renders proportionally.

nodes.name: draw_text
nodes.summary: Draws a line of words at a fixed position in a chosen font, routing to sprite glyphs on a tiled screen and to the framebuffer on a bitmap one.

nodes.name: draw_number
nodes.summary: Draws a whole number — a score, a timer, a counter — right-aligned in a fixed field with no leading zeros, dispatching to the fixed, live or tiled-HUD path depending on the value and the screen mode.

nodes.name: draw_live_number
nodes.summary: Draws a number that follows its variable: splits the value into digit places using hidden variables and paints one glyph per place, so the field updates itself every frame.

nodes.name: draw_text_tiled
nodes.summary: Draws text on a tiled screen, where there is no framebuffer, by declaring one small hardware-sprite glyph per character for the console to composite over the game.

nodes.name: draw_number_tiled
nodes.summary: Declares a live number as a row of hardware-sprite glyphs on a tiled screen, each glyph's pose following one digit place of the variable so the HUD updates itself.

nodes.name: glyph_image
nodes.summary: Renders and caches one character in one color as a single sprite tile, so a HUD reuses a glyph image instead of spending a tile per occurrence.

nodes.name: tiled.rb
nodes.summary: The tiled-background verbs `tiles` and `background`: say which character or sheet cell stands for which tile image, then stamp a grid of them from a heredoc map or a CSV tilemap exported by a map editor. Solid tiles are merged into wall rectangles so a sprite can be blocked by the level.

nodes.name: Tiled
nodes.summary: The tiled-background concern: two authoring routes for a tileset (by character, or a whole numbered sheet), two for a map (a heredoc, or a map editor's CSV), and the wall extraction that gives a level its collision.

nodes.name: tiles
nodes.summary: Defines a tileset two ways: a map from a character to the tile image it stands for, or a whole imported tile sheet numbered the way a map editor exports it. `solid:` marks which tiles are walls a sprite cannot move through.

nodes.name: background
nodes.summary: Stamps a grid of tiles from a heredoc map of tileset characters or from a CSV tilemap, and returns a handle that scrolls the visible window over it. The node carries the grid rather than a pile of draw calls, so a backend may stamp it by hand or give it to tile hardware.

nodes.name: define_sheet_tileset
nodes.summary: Imports a whole tile sheet as numbered tiles — 1, 2, 3 left to right — the exact numbering a map editor writes into a CSV export, so a level needs no characters at all.

nodes.name: char_image_grid
nodes.summary: Turns a character map — a heredoc or an array of row strings — into a grid of tile images, leaving a space as an empty cell.

nodes.name: csv_image_grid
nodes.summary: Turns a CSV tilemap of tile numbers into a grid of tile images, treating 0 as an empty cell.

nodes.name: parse_csv_tilemap
nodes.summary: Parses a map editor's CSV export into rows of tile numbers, reporting a ragged grid or a non-numeric cell as a plain build error.

nodes.name: merge_solid_cells
nodes.summary: Merges neighbouring solid tiles into as few wall rectangles as possible, so tile collision tests a handful of rectangles instead of every blocking cell.

nodes.name: timers.rb
nodes.summary: The `timer` verb: start a free-running hardware counter at a chosen rate and get a handle to read its ticks or stop it. It is the precise, frame-independent building block underneath the frame-paced `every` and `after` verbs.

nodes.name: Timers
nodes.summary: The timer concern: one verb, whose errors point a user who wanted frame-paced timing at `every` and `after` instead.

nodes.name: timer
nodes.summary: Starts a named hardware counter ticking a chosen number of times a second and returns a handle to read or stop it, pointing the user at `every` and `after` when they wanted frame-paced timing instead.

nodes.name: variables.rb
nodes.summary: The variable verbs: `var` declares state initialized once at boot, `save_var` declares state that survives power-off, and `set`, `add`, `sub`, `copy`, `negate`, `abs`, `clamp` and `approach` mutate it. Allocation itself stays in the builder core; these verbs record the operations and mirror every change of a persisted variable back to save memory.

nodes.name: Variables
nodes.summary: The variable concern: declaration, assignment and the small set of arithmetic moves a game actually needs, each returning a Value handle so the expression DSL can carry on from there.

nodes.name: set
nodes.summary: Assigns a variable at the point it is written, allocating it on first mention, mirroring the change to save memory if it is persisted, and returning a Value handle for the expression DSL.

nodes.name: var
nodes.summary: Declares a variable with a starting value applied once at boot, so declaring it inside a scene or a loop still initializes it a single time.

nodes.name: save_var
nodes.summary: Declares a variable whose value survives power-off — a high score, an unlock, a setting. It is used exactly like `var`, but lives in the cartridge's save memory and every change is written back automatically, with no separate save step.

nodes.name: add
nodes.summary: Adds a number, another variable, or an expression to a variable.

nodes.name: sub
nodes.summary: Subtracts a number, another variable, or an expression from a variable.

nodes.name: clamp
nodes.summary: Holds a variable between a minimum and a maximum — the usual way to keep a moving thing on screen or a value in range.

nodes.name: approach
nodes.summary: Moves a variable toward a target by at most one step per call and never overshoots — the chase-at-a-top-speed move behind a homing enemy, an easing camera or a tracking paddle. It is built branchlessly from a clamped delta.

nodes.name: constants.rb
nodes.summary: The one place raw Game Boy Advance hardware detail is allowed to live: memory-map base addresses, I/O register addresses, and control-register flag bits, named after the tonc/libgba conventions. Screen dimensions are not restated here — they are derived from the IR's shared Screen contract.
nodes.languageNotes: A Ruby module used purely as a namespaced constant table — no methods, only frozen address and flag values organized by hardware block.

nodes.name: ir.rb
nodes.summary: Entry point for the intermediate representation: requires every IR component in dependency order and documents the IR's core promise — a target-agnostic op-tree describing what a program does, not how one machine runs it.
nodes.languageNotes: A Ruby barrel file: `require_relative` pulls in the sibling files, and the module body holds only the explanatory documentation comment.

nodes.name: backends.rb
nodes.summary: Barrel that loads the two IR consumers — the Ruby interpreter and the GBA ROM lowering backend — and states the rule that every backend is downstream of the IR and must honor its reference semantics.
nodes.languageNotes: Backends are named for the platform they target (GBA, not Arm), so the namespace reads as a list of destinations rather than mechanisms.

nodes.name: ruby.rb
nodes.summary: The reference interpreter: runs an IR program directly in Ruby against simulated hardware — a fake framebuffer, a fake gamepad, an in-memory variable store, timers, and a software audio mixer. It is the project's headless test oracle, letting a test assert a pixel or a variable in-process with no emulator and no ROM.
nodes.languageNotes: One large class with a `case node.kind` dispatcher at its heart; the simulated hardware state is a set of instance-variable hashes documented inline in the constructor.

nodes.name: framebuffer.rb
nodes.summary: The interpreter's fake screen: a grid of color cells the draw operations write into and tests read back. Writes outside the grid are dropped silently, mirroring the edge-safety the DSL promises so a stray pixel can never corrupt state or crash a test.
nodes.languageNotes: Sizes itself from the shared IR Screen contract rather than repeating 240x160, so one change moves every backend.

nodes.name: list_value.rb
nodes.summary: The interpreter's model of a runtime list: a bounded, ordered collection supporting push, pop, shift, and indexed read/write. A plain Ruby array suffices because only the observable behavior — what fits, what overflows, what reads back — has to match the console's ring buffer.
nodes.languageNotes: The methods deliberately trust their caller; bounds checks live in the interpreter so a violation becomes a friendly error instead of a Ruby exception.

nodes.name: build.rb
nodes.summary: Readable constructors for every IR node kind — the surface the DSL and the tests build trees through. Each helper fixes one kind's operand names and routes value operands through `wrap`, so callers never learn the raw attribute conventions.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses `module_function` so helpers work either included or called as `Build.set(...)`; trailing underscores (`if_`, `loop_`, `case_`) dodge Ruby keywords.

nodes.name: buttons.rb
nodes.summary: The button vocabulary: the ten names a program may read with `held` or `pressed`. A cross-backend contract living in the IR core so every backend agrees on the same names and then maps each to its own world.

nodes.name: glyph_usage.rb
nodes.summary: Tree-shaking pass for fonts: walks a program to find which glyphs it can actually be asked to draw, per font, so only the reachable ones need embedding. Fixed text contributes its exact characters; a runtime number contributes the ten digits.

nodes.name: int32.rb
nodes.summary: The IR's reference integer semantics — signed 32-bit two's-complement with wraparound — defined once as a cross-backend contract every backend must honor. Pinning it here stops a float64-based backend from silently disagreeing with the register-based one on overflow, negative division, or signed comparison.
nodes.languageNotes: Division truncates toward zero like C and the console's BIOS, not like Ruby's `/` which floors — the divergence only bites on negatives, so it is fixed by dividing magnitudes and reapplying the sign.

nodes.name: modes.rb
nodes.summary: Resolves which screen mode each scene of a program runs in, by following the call graph from the per-frame entry points so a helper inherits its caller's mode. A routine reached from two different modes raises a friendly conflict instead of drawing the wrong way.
nodes.languageNotes: Pure structural analysis of the IR — the answer is computed once here so the lowering backend and the cost/palette passes cannot subtly disagree.

nodes.name: node.rb
nodes.summary: The IR node model: one plain-Ruby class covering both statement nodes (the program) and value nodes (expression operands), plus the CATEGORY table naming every op kind and its category. Control flow is structured nesting, so there are no labels or jumps — those are artifacts of flattening, left to the backend.
nodes.languageNotes: A single class serves both node shapes: children hold nested statements, while attrs hold operands (which may themselves be value nodes) — so the tree walks uniformly.

nodes.name: palette.rb
nodes.summary: Builds the color palette for indexed bitmap display automatically: walks a finished program, collects every distinct color it uses, and assigns each a table slot. This keeps the framework's promise that an author keeps naming colors and never learns what indexed color is.
nodes.languageNotes: Indexed color stores one byte per pixel instead of two, which is what leaves room for two full screens and makes tear-free double buffering possible — at a hard ceiling of 256 distinct colors, so overflow is a friendly build error.

nodes.name: portability.rb
nodes.summary: Tags every IR node kind as portable or hardware-only, and derives a whole program's tier as the floor over its nodes. This lets a preflight say up front that a program uses a hardware-only escape hatch, instead of a backend exploding partway through lowering.
nodes.languageNotes: The tag is per-kind and deliberately coarse; the north star is that `raw` stays the only hardware-only kind, since every other reach for it signals a missing IR node.

nodes.name: screen.rb
nodes.summary: The logical display contract: the screen's size in pixels, stated once in the IR core. The interpreter sizes its framebuffer from it, the hardware constants derive from it, and any future backend would size itself from it too.

nodes.name: verifier.rb
nodes.summary: Well-formedness pass that mechanically enforces the IR value model: a SLOTS table declares, per node kind, whether each field must hold a value node or an author-time literal, and the walk proves every verb wrapped its operands. A mismatch is a framework bug, so it raises InvariantError and is never shown to a game developer.
nodes.languageNotes: Deliberately distinct from the developer-facing guardrails: this catches a ruby-gba bug and offers no fix, where a guardrail finding reports a user's footgun in friendly language.

nodes.name: Constants
nodes.summary: Namespaced table of every Game Boy Advance hardware address and control-register flag the lower tiers need, grouped by hardware block (memory map, display, DMA, sound, timers, input).

nodes.name: Ruby
nodes.summary: The reference interpreter class: executes an IR tree against simulated hardware and exposes the result as inspectable state — variables, a framebuffer, an event log, audio events, and save memory. Bounded by a frame budget and a runaway step cap so a bad loop cannot hang a test.
nodes.languageNotes: Passing the same `save:` store to two runs models a power cycle, so persistence can be tested without a cartridge.

nodes.name: Framebuffer
nodes.summary: A grid of color cells standing in for the display: read and write single pixels, fill a rectangle, or clear the whole surface, with out-of-bounds writes dropped silently.

nodes.name: ListValue
nodes.summary: A capacity-bounded ordered collection backed by a Ruby array, exposing push, get, set, shift, pop, and the full/empty/index queries the interpreter checks before calling in.

nodes.name: Build
nodes.summary: One named constructor per IR node kind — variables, drawing, audio, control flow, timers, data, lists, tables, and expression values — each fixing that kind's operand names and coercing value operands into value nodes.

nodes.name: Buttons
nodes.summary: The shared list of the ten button names a program can read, plus the membership check callers use to turn a typo into a plain-language error rather than a button that reads as never pressed.

nodes.name: GlyphUsage
nodes.summary: Reports which glyph keys each font may actually be asked to draw in a program, and a per-font footprint summary that makes the tree-shaking visible.

nodes.name: Int32
nodes.summary: Signed 32-bit two's-complement arithmetic with wraparound: add, sub, mul, neg, truncating div, and signed compare, all routed through one wrap function so the meaning of overflow is defined in exactly one place.

nodes.name: Modes
nodes.summary: Resolves and answers questions about a program's screen modes: which mode each scene runs in, whether any scene is double-buffered or tiled, and whether the program mixes display systems.

nodes.name: Node
nodes.summary: A single IR node: a kind, its operand attrs, and its nested children, with the CATEGORY table classifying every kind and helpers to walk the tree, compare nodes, and render them for diagnostics.

nodes.name: Palette
nodes.summary: The built color-to-slot mapping for a program: collects distinct colors from the tree, reserves slot zero for black so a never-painted screen reads black for free, and answers index_of and entries for a backend to upload.

nodes.name: Portability
nodes.summary: The per-kind portability classification and the queries over it: whether a kind is portable or hardware-only, a program's overall tier, and which hardware-only kinds a program actually uses.

nodes.name: Verifier
nodes.summary: The well-formedness checker: walks a tree twice, first refusing unknown kinds, then checking every field against the SLOTS schema for that kind and confirming control-flow children really are statements.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Sets up the whole simulated machine in one place: variable store, fake screen, held buttons, frame counter, plus the registries for sounds, songs, samples, data blobs, bitmaps, objects, backgrounds, lists, tables, and timers.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: The interpreter's entry point: executes a program until it ends, halts, completes the requested number of frames, or exhausts the step budget, then returns self so a caller can inspect the result.

nodes.name: collect_definitions
nodes.summary: Pre-walks the tree to register every named definition — funcs, sounds, songs, data blobs, bitmaps, buffers, objects, backgrounds, samples, and tables — so a call or a trigger can refer to something defined later in the program.

nodes.name: tick!
nodes.summary: Charges one step against the budget and stops the run when it is exhausted, which is what keeps an accidental infinite loop from hanging a test forever.

nodes.name: exec
nodes.summary: The interpreter's core statement dispatcher: a single case over node kind that carries out every variable operation, drawing call, audio trigger, control-flow construct, timer action, and list mutation.
nodes.languageNotes: Refuses hardware-only kinds up front by asking IR::Portability, so an escape-hatch node fails with a clear message instead of being silently ignored.

nodes.name: advance_frame
nodes.summary: Completes one frame at the vblank boundary: records the edge state for press detection, applies scripted input, accrues timer overflows, advances sounding voices, and logs the vblank.
nodes.languageNotes: Vblank is the pause between drawn frames — the safe window to change what is on screen — so the interpreter models it as the one place per-frame bookkeeping happens.

nodes.name: advance_voices
nodes.summary: Ages every sounding sample by one frame, retiring voices that finished and restarting looping ones, so a test can watch several samples genuinely overlap in the mix.

nodes.name: paint_background_window
nodes.summary: Paints the visible window of a scrolling tiled background into the scene buffer, wrapping at the map edge so the world repeats the way the tile hardware would.

nodes.name: exec_present_objects
nodes.summary: Draws the declared moving objects for one frame, restoring what was under each one before redrawing it so a sprite leaves no trail — the software stand-in for hardware sprite compositing.

nodes.name: blit_image
nodes.summary: Copies a named bitmap onto the current draw target at a runtime position, skipping transparent pixels and clipping at the screen edges.

nodes.name: pixels_overlap?
nodes.summary: Shape-accurate collision test: gates on the two sprites' bounding boxes first, then confirms that solid pixels of the currently shown poses actually meet.

nodes.name: exec_restore_region
nodes.summary: Paints a previously saved patch of screen back where it came from, the second half of the save-under trick that lets a moving picture erase itself cleanly.

nodes.name: eval_node
nodes.summary: Evaluates a value node to a number: literals, variable reads, negation, binary operations, data and list and table reads, timer ticks, button reads, chance draws, and pixel-overlap tests.

nodes.name: eval_binop
nodes.summary: Applies one binary operator to two evaluated operands, routing arithmetic and every comparison through the shared 32-bit semantics so the interpreter cannot drift from the ROM backend.

nodes.name: wrap
nodes.summary: Coerces any operand into a value node — an author-time number folds to an int node, a symbol becomes a variable reference, an existing value node passes through — which is what lets every verb accept a literal or a runtime expression interchangeably.

nodes.name: reachable
nodes.summary: Walks a program and returns, per font, the sorted set of glyph keys it can be asked to draw — a fixed string contributes its own characters, a runtime number contributes the ten digits.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Indexes every func in the program, then resolves a mode for each per-frame entry point by walking outward from it, producing the scene-to-mode map the rest of the class answers from.

nodes.name: resolve_func
nodes.summary: Assigns a func its mode — the one it declares, or the one it was reached in — then recurses into everything it calls, raising a friendly conflict when a routine is reached from two different modes.

nodes.name: declared_mode
nodes.summary: Reads the mode a block of statements declares by finding its screen statement and mapping the requested kind and buffering choice onto one of the three modes.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Builds the color-to-slot table for a program: reserves slot zero for black, assigns a slot to each collected color in a stable order, and raises a friendly overflow error when the program names more colors than fit.

nodes.name: collect
nodes.summary: Gathers every distinct color a set of statement subtrees uses, taking colors both from drawing operations and from the pixel data of embedded bitmaps.

nodes.name: verify!
nodes.summary: The verifier's entry point: walks the tree once to reject unknown node kinds, then again to check every node's fields against its declared schema.

nodes.name: check_field
nodes.summary: Checks one field against its slot declaration — a value slot must hold a value node, a structural slot an author-time literal of the stated type — and raises an invariant error naming the offending verb when it does not.

nodes.name: mismatch_message
nodes.summary: Composes the diagnostic for a slot mismatch, choosing wording that tells a framework maintainer which direction the mistake ran — a raw literal in a value slot, or a runtime value in an author-time-only slot.

nodes.name: gba.rb
nodes.summary: The GBA backend's entry point: it walks a target-agnostic IR program and emits real ARM7 machine code for the console, in two passes so a jump into code that has not been written yet can be patched afterwards. It also decides where every variable lives in the console's fast work memory and prepares the program's pictures, tile maps, sprites and colour tables before a single instruction is emitted.
nodes.languageNotes: Ruby mixins are the file-splitting device here: one `GBA` class `include`s thirteen themed modules, so every `emit_*` helper shares the same instance state (the byte buffer, the label table, the variable map).

nodes.name: audio.rb
nodes.summary: Turns the sound verbs (beep, noise, wave, song) into short lists of writes to the console's four synthesized sound channels. Each op is first resolved to concrete musical values by the shared Sound module, so the ROM and the reference interpreter play the same notes.

nodes.name: bios_compress.rb
nodes.summary: Packs embedded artwork at build time into one of the two formats the console's own boot ROM knows how to expand, so the cartridge gets smaller and nothing extra is kept in scarce work memory. It tries a back-reference scheme and a run-length scheme, keeps whichever is smaller, and falls back to a plain copy when neither actually shrinks the data.

nodes.name: buffered.rb
nodes.summary: Drawing for the tear-free double-buffered screen, where the program draws into a hidden page while the TV shows the other one. A pixel here is one byte (an index into a colour table) instead of two, and video memory refuses a lone byte write, so every fill moves two pixels at once and must start on an even column.

nodes.name: collision.rb
nodes.summary: Shape-accurate sprite collision: once a cheap rectangle test says two sprites are near each other, this walks the area where they overlap and asks whether a drawn pixel of each lands on the same spot. It builds a one-byte-per-pixel solid/see-through table for every sprite pose at build time, so the test follows whichever animation frame is showing.

nodes.name: GBA
nodes.summary: The backend class itself: it holds the whole lowering state (emitted bytes, labels, variable addresses, embedded data blobs, sprite and background layouts, sound and timer bookkeeping) and mixes in the thirteen themed modules that do the actual emitting. `lower` runs the emit pass and then resolves every jump.
nodes.languageNotes: The register convention is documented at the top of the file: r0 is the accumulator, r1 a temporary and I/O address, r12 the variable-address scratch, and the CPU stack carries intermediates inside a nested expression. There is no register allocator yet.

nodes.name: Audio
nodes.summary: Sound lowering: each audio op becomes a short list of 16-bit writes to the sound registers. Songs are the interesting case — the note schedule is unrolled into a run-time frame comparison so the ROM plays the right note on the right frame without a scheduler.

nodes.name: BiosCompress
nodes.summary: Build-time asset packing with the two schemes the console's boot ROM can expand: LZ77 back-references (good for tile art, where small shapes recur) and run-length encoding (good for palettes and maps with long flat stretches). Every packed blob carries the 4-byte header the boot ROM reads, and packing can only help — an asset that does not shrink stays a plain copy.

nodes.name: Report
nodes.summary: An immutable value object holding one build's packing result — how many assets packed, their size before and after, and which schemes were used — and the one scannable summary line the build prints. The numbers are measured at build time, not estimated.

nodes.name: Buffered
nodes.summary: The double-buffered drawing path. It mirrors the direct-colour fills, but the destination is the hidden page whose address lives in a run-time variable and swaps on every flip, and everything moves in 16-bit units because a single-byte write to video memory would corrupt its neighbour.

nodes.name: Collision
nodes.summary: Per-pixel overlap testing, emitted inline where it is used. It keeps its working state (the two sprites' corners, their mask addresses, the overlap rectangle, the walk cursor, the answer) in a handful of hidden variables rather than juggling registers, because a collision test never runs nested inside another.

nodes.name: initialize
nodes.summary: Sets up every piece of lowering state in one place: the emitted byte buffer, the label and fixup tables, the variable-to-address map, and the bookkeeping for sounds, songs, data blobs, bitmaps, ROM tables, lists, samples, timers, backgrounds and sprites.

nodes.name: lower
nodes.summary: The whole compile in one method: collect definitions, prepare audio, timers, collision masks, screen modes, backgrounds and sprites, emit the boot setup, walk the program's statements, append the subroutines and data, then resolve every jump and return the finished machine code. Packaging it into a cartridge is the ROM layer's job.

nodes.name: resolve_modes
nodes.summary: Works out which screen mode each scene draws in by following the call graph from the program's entry points. A drawing helper reached in two different modes cannot be lowered both ways, so that conflict is surfaced as a friendly build error instead of a black screen.

nodes.name: collect_definitions
nodes.summary: A first walk over the whole program that registers everything a later emit needs to already know: defined sounds, songs, embedded data and images, ROM lookup tables, subroutines, lists and sprite backing stores.

nodes.name: emit_irq_setup
nodes.summary: Arms the interrupts the program needs. Waiting for the top of the frame asks the boot ROM to sleep the CPU until the next vertical blank rather than busy-poll the scanline counter, and that only works once the interrupt vector, the enable bits and the master switch are set up here.

nodes.name: emit_irq_handler
nodes.summary: The small interrupt routine the hardware vector points at: it works out which source fired, acknowledges it so the console will deliver the next one, and runs any timer handler the program attached.

nodes.name: prepare_backgrounds
nodes.summary: Resolves every declared tiled background into a concrete hardware layer: which background number it is, which block of video memory holds its map, its draw priority, and the one palette and tile block all the layers share.

nodes.name: prepare_one_background
nodes.summary: Turns one background's character map into the packed tile-number map the hardware reads, after checking the map fits the layer and every tile is the same size.

nodes.name: prepare_objects
nodes.summary: Resolves every declared hardware sprite into its slot in the console's sprite table, together with the tile data and palette entry it will be drawn from.

nodes.name: build_shared_object_palette
nodes.summary: Collects the colours used by every sprite into the one shared palette the sprite hardware reads, so the user only ever names colours and never manages a palette.

nodes.name: prepare_one_object
nodes.summary: Lays out one sprite: its size in 8x8 tile units, its slot in the sprite table, and the tile blob holding every pose, so a facing or animation change is only a change of which tile the hardware draws.

nodes.name: encode_object_tiles
nodes.summary: Rearranges a sprite's picture from plain rows of pixels into the 8x8 tile order the sprite hardware expects, packing two 4-bit colour indices per byte.

nodes.name: emit_play_song
nodes.summary: Lowers a song by unrolling its note schedule: a hidden frame counter advances each frame, and each note becomes a comparison that writes its sound-register values when the counter reaches that note's frame. Two voices can be layered, so a melody plays over a bass line.

nodes.name: build_song_tables
nodes.summary: Flattens a song's notes into a frame-indexed table of register writes, which is what makes the unrolled per-frame comparison possible.

nodes.name: emit_wait_vblank
nodes.summary: Waits for the safe drawing window at the top of the frame by asking the boot ROM to sleep the CPU until the next vertical blank, then snapshots the buttons and refills the sound mixer — the once-per-frame housekeeping every game loop needs.

nodes.name: best
nodes.summary: Packs a blob with both schemes and returns the smaller result, or reports that neither helped so the caller keeps the plain copy. This is why packing can never make a cartridge bigger.

nodes.name: lz77
nodes.summary: The sliding-window packer: a run of bytes that appeared a little earlier is written as a short 'copy N bytes from D bytes back' reference instead of the bytes themselves. It suits tile art, where the same small shapes and edges keep recurring.

nodes.name: rle
nodes.summary: The run-length packer: a byte repeated many times in a row is written once with a count. It suits palettes and maps with long flat stretches.

nodes.name: decode
nodes.summary: Expands a packed blob back to its original bytes by reading the 4-byte header to see which scheme was used. This mirrors what the console's boot ROM does at load time, so the build can verify a packed asset round-trips.

nodes.name: longest_match
nodes.summary: Searches the recent history for the longest run that repeats at the current position — the inner search that decides whether a back-reference is worth emitting.

nodes.name: decode_lz77
nodes.summary: Replays a back-reference stream: literal bytes are copied straight out, and each reference copies from what has already been expanded.

nodes.name: decode_rle
nodes.summary: Replays a run-length stream, expanding each repeat marker back into its run of identical bytes.

nodes.name: emit_clear_screen_buffered
nodes.summary: Clears the hidden page to a solid colour with one block transfer that repeats a packed word of four colour indices across the whole page.

nodes.name: emit_fill_rect_buffered
nodes.summary: Fills a fixed rectangle into the hidden page one row at a time, snapping the left edge to an even column because the tear-free screen moves two pixels per transfer.

nodes.name: emit_draw_rect_at_buffered
nodes.summary: Fills a fixed-size rectangle at a position only known at run time, computing the destination address in the hidden page and clipping each row against the screen edges as it goes.

nodes.name: emit_draw_text_buffered
nodes.summary: Draws text into the hidden page by writing the colour-table index of each lit glyph pixel, since the tear-free screen stores an index per pixel rather than a colour.

nodes.name: emit_plot_digit_index
nodes.summary: Plots one pixel of a live number into the hidden page at a run-time position, splicing the byte into its 16-bit slot without disturbing the neighbouring pixel.

nodes.name: emit_pixel_buffered
nodes.summary: Writes one pixel into the hidden page, taking the constant-position fast path when the coordinates are known at build time.

nodes.name: emit_pixel_buffered_runtime
nodes.summary: Writes one pixel at a run-time position into the hidden page: compute the byte address, read the 16-bit slot it shares with its neighbour, splice in the new index, and write the slot back.

nodes.name: mask_bytes
nodes.summary: Builds a sprite pose's solid-pixel table — one byte per pixel, 1 where the art is drawn and 0 where it is see-through — which is the data the per-pixel test reads at run time.

nodes.name: eval_pixels_overlap
nodes.summary: Emits a complete per-pixel overlap test: stash both sprites' corners and mask addresses, compute the rectangle where their boxes intersect, and walk it looking for a spot where both are drawn. Leaves 1 or 0 in the accumulator.

nodes.name: walk_overlap
nodes.summary: The inner double loop over the overlapping rectangle, emitted inline: for each spot, read both sprites' mask bytes and stop early the moment two drawn pixels meet.

nodes.name: load_mask_byte
nodes.summary: Reads one byte of a sprite's solid-pixel table at the current walk position, converting the spot on screen into an offset inside that sprite's own picture.

nodes.name: direct_sound.rb
nodes.summary: The hardware layer for recorded (sampled) audio, as opposed to the synthesized beeps. It embeds each clip's raw sound data in the cartridge and holds the settings for the one channel, memory-transfer engine and timer that stream bytes out at the playback rate; adding several clips together is the software mixer's job.

nodes.name: drawing.rb
nodes.summary: The largest lowering module: everything that puts a picture on the direct-colour screen — single pixels, filled rectangles, images with see-through pixels, text glyphs and live numbers — plus the screen-mode and page management around it. It also uploads tile sets, tile maps and hardware sprites, and drives the console's block-copy engine for the fast fills.

nodes.name: emit.rb
nodes.summary: The lowest layer of the backend: append bytes to the growing machine-code buffer, record a named position (a label), and write a jump as a fixed-size placeholder that is patched into a real distance once every label's position is known. This two-pass trick is what lets the backend emit a jump forward into code it has not written yet.

nodes.name: expressions.rb
nodes.summary: Lowers anything that produces a value — numbers, variable reads, arithmetic, comparisons, ROM table lookups, list reads and button state — leaving the answer in the accumulator register. Comparisons become a conditional set, and button reads translate the console's active-low key register into plain 1-means-down logic, including press-edge detection.

nodes.name: lists.rb
nodes.summary: Runtime-sized lists, laid out as ring buffers in the console's fast work memory with hidden head and length variables. Capacity is a power of two so the wrap-around is a single bitwise AND with no division, which also confines a bad index to the list's own block instead of a neighbouring variable. It also holds the sprite save-under memory and the subroutine/case machinery.

nodes.name: DirectSound
nodes.summary: The sampled-audio hardware layer: register the program's clips as ROM data, and hold the channel, transfer-engine and timer settings that stream one 8-bit sound stream out of a small queue at the playback rate.

nodes.name: Drawing
nodes.summary: Direct-colour drawing plus all the screen-mode and page management around it. Every entry point checks the mode it is lowering in and hands off to the double-buffered variant when needed, so one IR node lowers correctly whichever screen a scene picked.

nodes.name: Emit
nodes.summary: Byte emission and the two-pass label/branch fixup machinery. A branch is always 4 bytes no matter how far it jumps, so emitting a placeholder never shifts any later position — which is exactly why the second pass can patch jumps without re-laying-out the program.

nodes.name: Expressions
nodes.summary: Value-node evaluation: every expression lowers to code that leaves its result in the accumulator register, so nested expressions compose by pushing intermediates on the CPU stack.

nodes.name: Lists
nodes.summary: The memory layout and operations for lists and the sprite save-under store, plus subroutine emission and case dispatch. The ring-buffer layout mirrors the interpreter's list exactly, so both backends agree on what is readable and where it overflows.

nodes.name: prepare_direct_sound
nodes.summary: Walks the program to embed every recorded clip's raw sound data in the cartridge and notes whether anything is ever played, which is what tells the backend to bring the mixer up at boot.

nodes.name: emit_screen
nodes.summary: Turns the screen on by writing the chosen mode to the display-control register — until this runs the screen stays black. In a program that switches modes per scene it emits nothing, because the display is managed centrally at boot and on each scene transition instead.

nodes.name: emit_flip
nodes.summary: Swaps the two pages of the tear-free screen: toggle the one display-control bit that chooses which page the TV shows, and point the drawing address at the other one. The TV never reads a half-drawn page, so the picture cannot tear.

nodes.name: emit_pixel
nodes.summary: Writes one pixel, taking a build-time-constant address when the coordinates are known and computing it at run time otherwise, and handing off to the double-buffered path when the scene draws tear-free.

nodes.name: emit_fill_rect
nodes.summary: Fills a rectangle whose position and size are fixed at build time, emitting the row writes directly.

nodes.name: emit_clear_screen
nodes.summary: Clears the whole screen with a single block transfer: pack two copies of the colour into one 32-bit word and let the console's copy engine repeat it across every pixel.

nodes.name: emit_dma_fill_rect
nodes.summary: Fills a fixed rectangle with the console's block-copy engine, one transfer per row, which is far faster than writing the pixels one at a time.

nodes.name: emit_draw_rect_at
nodes.summary: Fills a fixed-size rectangle at a position only known at run time, computing the address of each row and clipping rows that fall off the screen.

nodes.name: emit_scroll_background
nodes.summary: Moves the visible window over a tiled background by writing its scroll registers, which is how a world slides under a centred hero for free.

nodes.name: pack_blob
nodes.summary: Packs an embedded asset before it goes into the cartridge and records which scheme was used, so the loader knows whether to copy it plainly or ask the boot ROM to expand it.

nodes.name: emit_present_object
nodes.summary: Writes one hardware sprite's entry in the console's sprite table each frame: its position, its size and shape, and which tile it is drawn from. The console composites it over the background for free.

nodes.name: emit_object_tile_number
nodes.summary: Works out at run time which tile a sprite should be drawn from, which is how a facing change or an animation frame becomes a single number the hardware reads.

nodes.name: emit_rect_row_dma
nodes.summary: The shared row-copy engine behind image drawing and sprite save-under: copy a rectangle row by row between a ROM or RAM buffer and the screen, clipping at run time. A row past a side edge is trimmed to its visible span, without which it would wrap onto the next line.

nodes.name: emit_blit_transparent
nodes.summary: Draws an image with see-through pixels by unrolling it at build time: emit a store only for the pixels that are actually drawn, each with its colour baked in and guarded by a run-time screen-bounds check, so the background shows through the rest.

nodes.name: emit_draw_text
nodes.summary: Draws text at a fixed position by walking the font's glyph pixels and writing each lit one, handing off to the double-buffered path when the scene draws tear-free.

nodes.name: emit_draw_digit
nodes.summary: Draws one digit of a live number, choosing the cheapest form available: fully unrolled when the position and font width are known at build time, or a glyph loop when they are not.

nodes.name: emit_digit_glyph_loop
nodes.summary: The general run-time digit renderer: look the digit's glyph up in a build-time table and plot its lit pixels, used when the position is not known until the game runs.

nodes.name: resolve_fixups
nodes.summary: The second pass: now that every label's byte position is known, rewrite each 4-byte jump placeholder as a real branch to its target. This is what makes forward jumps possible without hand-computed distances.

nodes.name: resolve_branch
nodes.summary: Turns one placeholder into a real branch by measuring the distance from the jump to its label and encoding it, keeping the conditional and call forms distinct.

nodes.name: eval_value
nodes.summary: The value dispatcher: every kind of expression node — a number, a variable read, negation, arithmetic, a button read, a random chance, a collision test, a table or list read, the scanline counter — lowers to code that leaves its result in the accumulator register.

nodes.name: eval_table_get
nodes.summary: Reads a build-time lookup table shipped in the cartridge at a run-time index, making an out-of-range index safe: a power-of-two table wraps it (what an angle wants) and any other size clamps to the ends.

nodes.name: emit_clamp_acc
nodes.summary: Clamps whatever is in the accumulator to a range using conditional moves, so no jump is needed.

nodes.name: eval_binop
nodes.summary: Lowers a two-operand expression: evaluate the left side, push it, evaluate the right, then combine them. Multiplication uses the CPU's multiply instruction and division falls back to an emitted routine, since the CPU has none.

nodes.name: emit_comparison
nodes.summary: Turns a comparison into a 0 or 1 in the accumulator by setting the result and then conditionally clearing it under the inverse condition — no jump required.

nodes.name: eval_held
nodes.summary: Reads whether a button is down right now. The console's key register is active-low, so a 0 bit means pressed; this flips that into the plain 1-means-down answer the program expects.

nodes.name: eval_pressed
nodes.summary: Detects the moment a button goes down, by comparing this frame's button snapshot with the previous frame's — down now and up last frame. Both snapshots are taken once per frame so every check inside a frame agrees.

nodes.name: register_list
nodes.summary: Reserves a list's memory: a block of 4-byte slots plus the hidden head and length variables. Declaring the same name twice with different capacities is a contradiction and is refused.

nodes.name: register_backing
nodes.summary: Reserves the save-under buffer a software sprite needs — the patch of screen it covers, kept so the sprite can be erased next frame without leaving a trail.

nodes.name: emit_list_push
nodes.summary: Appends an item to a list: work out the physical slot from head plus length, write the value, and bump the length — with the wrap done by a single bitwise AND.

nodes.name: emit_list_drop
nodes.summary: Removes an item from either end of a list, advancing the head for a shift or just shortening the length for a pop.

nodes.name: emit_functions
nodes.summary: Emits every subroutine after the main body, recording each one's byte span so a build can disassemble it later, and wrapping each in the save-and-return pair that lets it be called from anywhere.

nodes.name: mixer.rb
nodes.summary: A software mixer that lets several recorded clips sound at once, which the hardware cannot do on its own — it plays only one stream. Each frame the CPU sums every playing voice into a buffer while the transfer engine plays the other, then swaps them, so the hardware never reads a half-written buffer. A voice steps through its clip at a fractional rate, which is how one recording plays at different pitches.

nodes.name: primitives.rb
nodes.summary: The small shared helpers every other lowering module leans on: hand a variable its 4-byte slot in fast work memory on first mention, load and store it, write a 16- or 32-bit value to a hardware register, fold a build-time constant, and check a coordinate against the screen.

nodes.name: save.rb
nodes.summary: Lowers the persistence ops to the battery-backed memory chip on the cartridge, which keeps its contents while the console is off. That chip sits on an 8-bit bus, so a 4-byte value is read and written one byte at a time, and the ROM must carry a marker string an emulator or flashcart scans for before it will map the chip in at all.

nodes.name: statements.rb
nodes.summary: The statement dispatcher, plus the variable ops and control-flow shapes that have no module of their own: assignment, add/subtract, copy, negate, absolute value, clamp, and if/loop/repeat/every/after. A conditional is emitted as an inverse-condition jump that skips the block, so nothing has to stay live in a register across a statement.

nodes.name: timers.rb
nodes.summary: Assigns each named timer one of the console's four hardware counters and works out the prescaler and reload value that give the rate the program asked for. A timer whose overflow count is read also reserves the counter immediately after it in cascade mode, because a raw counter races too fast to read meaningfully — the cascade partner counts the overflows instead.

nodes.name: Mixer
nodes.summary: The software mixer: a fixed number of voice slots in fast work memory, a per-frame refill that sums every sounding voice into the buffer the hardware is not currently playing, and the buffer swap. A play past the last free slot is dropped quietly rather than stealing a voice that is already sounding.

nodes.name: Primitives
nodes.summary: Shared low-level helpers: variable addressing in fast work memory, loads and stores, hardware-register writes, build-time constant folding, and a screen-bounds check.

nodes.name: Save
nodes.summary: Save-memory lowering. The layout is a 4-byte marker followed by one 4-byte slot per persisted variable; the marker is what tells a fresh cartridge full of uninitialized garbage apart from one that already holds real saved data.

nodes.name: Statements
nodes.summary: Statement lowering: the big dispatch on node kind, the variable-mutation ops, and the control-flow shapes. Every branch target is a generated label resolved in the second pass, so no jump distance is ever computed by hand.

nodes.name: Timers
nodes.summary: Hardware timer allocation and configuration. Each of the console's four counters ticks at the CPU clock divided by a prescaler and overflows past 65535; picking the reload value is what sets the rate the program asked for.

nodes.name: prepare_mixer
nodes.summary: Works out the mixer's output rate, reserves its two sound buffers and its voice slots in work memory, and claims the one hardware timer that clocks playback.

nodes.name: emit_mixer_boot
nodes.summary: Brings the sound path up at boot: clear the buffers to silence, configure the sound channel and its transfer engine, and start the timer whose overflow rate is the playback rate.

nodes.name: emit_play_sample
nodes.summary: Starts a clip sounding by filling a free voice slot with where its data lives, how long it is, whether it loops, its volume and its pitch step. With no free slot the play is dropped quietly rather than cutting off something already sounding.

nodes.name: emit_mixer_tick
nodes.summary: The per-frame refill: fill whichever buffer is not currently playing with the next slice of mixed sound, then point the hardware at it so it plays next. Which buffer is which is held in a hidden variable and flipped every frame.

nodes.name: emit_mix_into
nodes.summary: The heart of the mixer: fill a buffer with the sum of every sounding voice, clamped to the 8-bit range so loud moments do not wrap around into noise. Each voice is scaled by its volume and stepped through its clip by a fixed-point rate, then advanced and either looped or retired at its end.

nodes.name: find_free_slot
nodes.summary: Scans the voice slots for one that is not sounding, which is what makes a play past the voice limit a safe no-op instead of a stolen voice.

nodes.name: emit_zero_region
nodes.summary: Clears a block of work memory to silence, used to start each mix from a clean buffer.

nodes.name: var_addr
nodes.summary: Hands a variable its own 4-byte slot in the console's fast work memory the first time it is mentioned. This backend, not the DSL, decides where a variable lives, which is why the address map it produces is what a hardware test reads values back from.

nodes.name: emit_save_init
nodes.summary: At boot, load the persisted values back or seed a fresh cartridge with the defaults. It is written without a jump: one compare of the stored marker decides, through conditional instructions, whether each value is kept or replaced.

nodes.name: emit_save_store
nodes.summary: Writes one persisted variable back to the cartridge's save chip, one byte at a time because that memory sits on an 8-bit bus. Every change is saved automatically, so the program never needs a separate save step.

nodes.name: emit_statement
nodes.summary: The backend's main dispatch: one case over every statement node kind, routing to the module that lowers it — variable ops, control flow, lists, drawing, sound, timers, saves, and the raw escape hatch. A kind with no case is a friendly build error rather than silence.

nodes.name: emit_clamp
nodes.summary: Keeps a variable inside a range by comparing against each end and conditionally replacing it, so nothing jumps.

nodes.name: emit_if
nodes.summary: Lowers a conditional by evaluating the test and emitting an inverse-condition jump that skips over the block, with a second jump around the else side when there is one.

nodes.name: emit_repeat
nodes.summary: Lowers a counted loop: set up a hidden counter, emit the body once, then a compare and a backward jump — so the loop costs one copy of the body no matter how many times it runs.

nodes.name: register_timer
nodes.summary: Gives one named timer its hardware counter, and reserves the counter immediately after it as a cascade partner when the program reads that timer's overflow count.

nodes.name: emit_timer_start
nodes.summary: Starts a timer by writing its reload value and control bits, and starts the cascade partner too when there is one so the overflow count begins from zero.

nodes.name: timer_config
nodes.summary: Picks the finest prescaler whose overflow period still fits a 16-bit counter and computes the reload value that gives the requested rate — the arithmetic that turns 'sixty times a second' into hardware settings.

nodes.name: shmup.rb
nodes.summary: Entry point of the vertical shoot-'em-up showcase: builds the SHMUP ROM on a tiled screen and dispatches between two scenes each frame with case_var. The PLAYING scene constructs the Player, Enemies, and Hud parts, so their sprites and HUD text belong to that scene and disappear on the GAME OVER screen with no per-draw visibility flag.
nodes.languageNotes: Composition with no framework base class: `RubyGBA.game` yields the builder as `self`, and each part is an ordinary Ruby object constructed with that builder — `Player.new(self)` — which then calls DSL verbs on it.

nodes.name: player.rb
nodes.summary: The player's ship and its single shot as one part of the multi-file game: declares both sprites from ASCII art, steers with held(:left)/held(:right), pins the ship on screen with clamp_to_screen, and fires one shot at a time on the A button. Shows a game part written as a plain Ruby object that takes the build and calls DSL verbs on it.
nodes.languageNotes: Sprite art is a heredoc of ASCII characters mapped to color names (`"." => :transparent, "#" => :cyan`), so the reader never touches a palette or tile format.

nodes.name: enemies.rb
nodes.summary: The enemy squadron: three sprites drawn from ASCII art that drift down, respawn at a random column when they pass the bottom, and resolve collisions with the player's shot (score and free the shot) and with the ship (cost a life). The Ruby `each` runs at build time, so the same behavior is simply unrolled once per enemy with no runtime indexing.
nodes.languageNotes: A build-time `Array.new(COUNT)` / `each` is code generation, not a runtime loop — each enemy's logic is emitted separately into the frame, which is why a fixed count is used here instead of a runtime collection.

nodes.name: hud.rb
nodes.summary: The heads-up display: owns the score and lives variables and declares the tiled-mode text and live numbers that repaint themselves from those variables every frame. Exposes score_up, hit, and reset so the other parts change the display without knowing how it is drawn.
nodes.languageNotes: In tiled mode `draw_text` / `draw_number` are set-and-forget: declared once inside a scene, each glyph becomes a hardware sprite the console composites every frame, and a live number follows its variable.

nodes.name: Player
nodes.summary: Holds the ship sprite, the shot sprite, and the shot_live flag that keeps exactly one shot in flight. Exposes update (one frame of steering and firing), reclaim_shot (used by Enemies when a shot lands), reset, and readers for ship/shot so other parts can test collisions.

nodes.name: Enemies
nodes.summary: Creates three enemy sprites spread across the top at staggered heights and drives them each frame: drift down, wrap round from the bottom, and handle the two collisions that matter (shot hits enemy, enemy hits ship). Takes the Player and the Hud in update because those are the collaborators it acts on.

nodes.name: Hud
nodes.summary: Declares the SCORE and SHIPS readouts and owns their two variables. score_up adds ten, hit removes a life and clamps it so two collisions on one frame cannot break the display, and lives is read by the main file to end the game.

nodes.name: update
nodes.summary: One frame of the ship: move left or right while the button is held, clamp to the screen using the sprite's own size, then run the fire and shot-flight steps.

nodes.name: fire_when_ready
nodes.summary: Fires on the A press edge only when no shot is in flight: places the shot at the ship's nose, shows it, and raises the shot_live flag so a second shot cannot start.

nodes.name: update
nodes.summary: One frame for every enemy: move it down, respawn it when it goes below the bottom, score and reclaim the shot when a live shot overlaps it, and cost a life when it touches the ship.

nodes.name: make_example_assets.rb
nodes.summary: Developer script that regenerates the checked-in example art from plain pixel data rather than committing opaque binaries. Running it writes examples/assets/tiles.png (an 8x8 brick plus floor tile sheet), hero.png (a four-frame 16x16 walk cycle cut out on alpha) and level.csv (a 30x20 tilemap in the format a map editor exports), which examples/sheet.rb and examples/level.rb then import.
nodes.languageNotes: A `module_function` module rather than a class: every method is callable on the module and the file self-executes only when run directly (`__FILE__ == $PROGRAM_NAME`). PNGs are encoded by hand over Ruby's built-in zlib, so the repo needs no image library.

nodes.name: make_piano_assets.rb
nodes.summary: Developer script that generates the art and sound examples/piano.rb imports: seven 64x32 cut-out hand sprites (a resting pose plus one per pressed finger for the right hand, resting plus a two-finger block chord for the left) and piano.wav, a synthesized 0.6s C4 note the `instrument` verb pitches across the keyboard.
nodes.languageNotes: The note is synthesized in pure Ruby — a fundamental plus two quieter harmonics under an exponential decay envelope — then packed into a minimal RIFF/WAVE container with `Array#pack`, so no audio library is needed.

nodes.name: preview.rb
nodes.summary: Runs an example program on the Ruby reference interpreter, captures each settled frame, and writes a self-contained HTML page that plays those frames back on a canvas, so motion (scrolling, parallax, animation) can be watched without an emulator or hardware. Doubles as the repo's shared PNG encoder — its `png`, `chunk` and `rgb` helpers are reused by both asset-generation scripts.
nodes.languageNotes: Three concerns in one module: driving the interpreter through its `each_vblank` hook (aborting the endless game loop with `throw :halt` once enough frames are captured), a hand-rolled truecolor PNG codec over zlib, and an HTML/JS player emitted from a heredoc. Examples are loaded reflectively — the file name is camel-cased into a constant looked up with `Object.const_get`.

nodes.name: MakeExampleAssets
nodes.summary: Module holding the whole example-asset pipeline: the ASCII room layout, the 5-bit console palette used for brick, floor and hero pixels, and the drawing and encoding methods that turn them into files.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Entry point: creates examples/assets if missing, then writes tiles.png, hero.png and level.csv and reports what it wrote.

nodes.name: level_csv
nodes.summary: Converts the ASCII LEVEL room into a CSV tilemap, mapping '#' to tile 1 (brick) and everything else to tile 2 (floor) — the exact shape a map editor exports, so examples/level.rb can import it unchanged.

nodes.name: tiles_png
nodes.summary: Builds the 16x8 two-cell tile sheet — an 8x8 brick in the left cell, an 8x8 floor in the right — and encodes it as an opaque RGB PNG through the preview tool's encoder.

nodes.name: brick_pixel
nodes.summary: Returns the color of one pixel of the brick tile: mortar on the horizontal courses and on a staggered vertical seam, brick everywhere else, giving a running-bond pattern with a solid interior.

nodes.name: hero_png
nodes.summary: Builds the 64x16 sprite sheet of four 16x16 walk frames on a fully transparent background and encodes it as an RGBA PNG, so the imported sprite is a clean cut-out.

nodes.name: draw_hero_frame
nodes.summary: Draws one walk frame into the sheet at a column offset: a fixed head-and-torso block with two eyes, plus legs in one of two alternating stances so the four frames read as a walk cycle.

nodes.name: rgba_png
nodes.summary: Encodes an RGBA (color type 6) PNG by expanding each 15-bit console color to 8-bit channels and appending a per-pixel alpha byte, reusing the preview tool's chunk writer and PNG signature.

nodes.name: MakePianoAssets
nodes.summary: Module holding the piano example's asset pipeline: the hand's geometry (palm bounds, four finger centers, resting tip lengths per hand), the skin/outline/nail palette, the note's rate and pitch, and the drawing, synthesis and encoding methods.

nodes.name: run
nodes.summary: Entry point: writes the right hand's resting pose plus one pose per pressed finger, the left hand's resting and block-chord poses, and the piano.wav note, all into examples/assets.

nodes.name: hand_png
nodes.summary: Draws one 64x32 hand pose on a transparent background and encodes it as an RGBA PNG. The `pressed` list picks which fingers stab down to the common key row; `rest_tips` gives the others their natural lengths, which is what makes it read as a left or right hand.

nodes.name: draw_palm
nodes.summary: Draws the back of the hand as a filled block outlined on the top and sides, leaving the bottom open so the fingers merge into it seamlessly.

nodes.name: draw_finger
nodes.summary: Draws one finger from the palm down to a given tip row: outlined on both sides, tapered to a rounded fingertip, with side shading, a knuckle crease and a pale nail. A longer tip is what renders the finger as pressed.

nodes.name: piano_wav
nodes.summary: Synthesizes a plucked, decaying piano-like note — a fundamental plus two quieter harmonics under an exponential envelope — as 8-bit signed samples, then wraps them in a WAV container.

nodes.name: wav_bytes
nodes.summary: Wraps signed 8-bit samples in a minimal mono PCM RIFF/WAVE container, recentering them to the unsigned 0..255 range WAV expects for 8-bit audio.

nodes.name: rgba_png
nodes.summary: Encodes an RGBA (color type 6) PNG from 15-bit console colors plus a per-pixel alpha byte, reusing the preview tool's chunk writer so the hands read back as exact console colors, cut out where transparent.

nodes.name: Preview
nodes.summary: Module exposing the whole preview pipeline as module methods: capture frames from the reference interpreter, encode them to PNG data URIs, emit a standalone HTML player, and load an example by name from the command line.

nodes.name: capture
nodes.summary: Runs a program on the Ruby reference interpreter and collects the first N settled frames as {width:, height:, pixels:} hashes. An optional block supplies the buttons held each frame, and the run is cut short with `throw :halt` once enough frames are captured.

nodes.name: write
nodes.summary: Writes the captured frames to a self-contained HTML page at the given path and returns that path.

nodes.name: html
nodes.summary: Renders the captured frames as HTML: every frame inlined as a PNG data URI plus a small canvas player with play/pause and a scrub slider. Returns a full document, or just the body when `fragment: true` for embedding.

nodes.name: png
nodes.summary: Encodes a frame as an 8-bit truecolor PNG: each 15-bit BGR555 color is expanded to 8-bit RGB, scanlines get a leading no-filter byte, and the result is deflated into a single IDAT chunk. Also used by both asset-generation scripts.

nodes.name: chunk
nodes.summary: Builds one PNG chunk — length, type, data and a CRC32 over the type and data — the shared primitive every PNG writer in the repo appends with.

nodes.name: rgb
nodes.summary: Expands a 15-bit BGR555 console color into 8-bit-per-channel RGB, replicating the top bits so full scale stays full scale. Shared by both asset scripts so generated files round-trip to the exact console colors.

nodes.name: load_example
nodes.summary: Requires examples/NAME.rb and returns its module, found by camel-casing the file name and looking the constant up. Raises a clear error when the file is missing or the module exposes no `.program`.

nodes.name: run_cli
nodes.summary: Command-line driver: loads the named example, captures its program with the held keys and step budget, writes the HTML preview, and returns the output path.

nodes.name: ci.yml
nodes.summary: Manually dispatched GitHub Actions workflow that runs the project's test suites on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ruby 4.0: it apt-installs a C toolchain plus libmgba and ImageMagick, runs `bundle exec rake test` (which builds gemba-core's C extension first), then runs gemba-core's own `rake test:mgba` suite, and uploads both logs as artifacts. It gates nothing automatically — there is no push or pull-request trigger, so it only runs on demand.
nodes.languageNotes: Two details are specific to this project. The workflow is `workflow_dispatch` only, so it never fires on push or PR — CI is opt-in. And it apt-installs `libmgba-dev` plus a compiler because the emulator-backed pixel tests build gemba-core's C extension against a system libmgba; the probe is headless, so no display server, SDL2, or audio daemon is needed.

nodes.name: README.md
nodes.summary: Main project introduction for ruby-gba, a Ruby DSL that compiles plain Ruby into real Game Boy Advance ROMs. It opens with a worked Snake example, then covers the design pillars (hide the hardware, guardrails as teaching errors, the value-centric expression DSL, the IR with its GBA and Ruby backends, and the `rom.explain` cost estimator), a working/planned feature checklist, a table describing every runnable example, and the lib/ directory layout.
nodes.languageNotes: The README doubles as the architecture map: its "Project layout" block is the canonical description of how lib/ruby_gba/ is split (DSL surface, value model, IR + backends, ARM encoding, verifier), and the examples table names which drawing strategy each demo teaches.

nodes.name: AGENTS.md
nodes.summary: Contributor guide written for AI agents working in this repository. It points at bd (beads) as the single task tracker, gives a command quick-reference, lists non-interactive shell forms that stop an agent from hanging on confirmation prompts, and defines a mandatory session-completion workflow that is not finished until `git push` succeeds.

nodes.name: LICENSE.md
nodes.summary: MIT license for the project plus two notices specific to a Game Boy Advance toolchain: a Nintendo trademark disclaimer stating the tool is unofficial and unaffiliated, and an explanation that the Nintendo boot logo written into every ROM header is reproduced for interoperability only and is explicitly excluded from the MIT grant.
nodes.languageNotes: The boot-logo carve-out is a real hardware constraint, not boilerplate. The GBA BIOS refuses to start a cartridge unless bytes 0x04-0x9F of its header hold a specific 156-byte Nintendo logo bitmap, so any tool that produces bootable ROMs must ship those bytes — here as `HEADER_LOGO_BYTES` in lib/ruby_gba/constants.rb.

nodes.name: commit-msg
nodes.summary: Git commit-msg hook that rejects any commit message containing a beads tracker id (the lowercase `gba-<id>` form), keeping internal process ids out of permanent git history. It strips comment lines first and tells the author to describe the change instead, with `git commit --no-verify` as the escape hatch.
nodes.languageNotes: POSIX sh so it runs anywhere git does; the grep is case-sensitive on purpose so prose like "GBA-based" is not a false positive.

nodes.name: Gemfile
nodes.summary: Bundler manifest for the project. It declares rubygems.org as the source and delegates every dependency to the gemspec, so `ruby-gba.gemspec` stays the single place dependencies are declared.

nodes.name: Rakefile
nodes.summary: Build and test entry point. Its default task is `test`, which first builds gemba-core's C extension (the vendored headless libmgba probe the emulator-backed tests need) as a Rake file task, then runs every `test/**/test_*.rb`. It also exposes `test:mgba` for gemba-core's own suite and `rake preview EXAMPLE=…` to render an example to a watchable HTML page.
nodes.languageNotes: The extension binary is modeled as a Rake *file task* keyed on its C sources, so a plain `rake test` recompiles only when a source is newer — the compile takes longer than the suite itself. A failed build stops the suite loudly rather than letting it pass with gutted coverage.

nodes.name: ruby-gba
nodes.summary: The `ruby-gba` command-line executable shim. It prepends the checkout's `lib/` to the load path (so the CLI runs from a working copy, not only from the installed gem), then hands ARGV to the Thor CLI class in `lib/ruby_gba/cli.rb`.

nodes.name: level.csv
nodes.summary: A 30x20 tilemap exported in the CSV format a map editor like Tiled produces — one row per line, each cell a tile number (1 = brick wall, 2 = floor, 0 would be an empty cell). It is the level data loaded by `examples/level.rb` through the `background :room, tiles: :world, from: "level.csv"` verb.
nodes.languageNotes: The map is a solid brick border with interior pillar blocks — shaped to show off tile collision and scrolling rather than to be a real level.

nodes.name: image.rb
nodes.summary: The image-import subsystem: turns a real picture file on the host machine (PNG, JPG, …) into a flat, row-major list of console colors the framework can embed in a ROM and draw with `blit`. It handles whole images, alpha cutouts (see-through pixels become a transparent marker) and sprite/tile sheets sliced into equal cells or arbitrary rectangles, all behind a swappable adapter so nothing else in the framework shells out to an image tool.
nodes.languageNotes: The public surface is `module_function` on `RubyGBA::Image`, so callers write `Image.load(...)`. `Bitmap` is a `Data.define` value object — plain data that knows nothing about ROMs or hardware. `TRANSPARENT` is 0x8000, the unused 16th bit of a 15-bit color, so the see-through marker can never collide with a real color.

nodes.name: image_magick.rb
nodes.summary: The ImageMagick adapter — the one place the project shells out to an external image tool. It drives `magick` (or the older `convert`) to resize-and-crop a picture to an exact size and dump the raw RGB or RGBA channel bytes to stdout, and to read an image's own dimensions from its header without loading pixels.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses Open3.capture3 with binmode so raw pixel bytes survive intact. The adapter deliberately knows nothing about the GBA — it returns plain 8-bit channels and the color conversion happens in image.rb, which keeps the tool swappable.

nodes.name: ruby-gba.gemspec
nodes.summary: Gem packaging manifest for `ruby-gba`. It reads the version from `lib/ruby_gba/version.rb`, ships `lib/`, `test/` and `bin/`, wires `bin/ruby-gba` as the gem's executable, requires Ruby 3.2+, and declares Thor as the only runtime dependency (Rake and Minitest are development-only).

nodes.name: Sheet
nodes.summary: One decoded picture holding a grid of equal-size cells — a tile sheet or a sprite sheet. It keeps the whole sheet's raw pixel bytes once and hands back any single cell or rectangle as a ready-to-use Bitmap, so a sheet of many tiles is decoded a single time instead of once per tile.

nodes.name: cell
nodes.summary: Returns the sheet cell at a zero-based column and row as a Bitmap of the sheet's tile size, converting each pixel on the way out. An out-of-grid cell raises a plain-language error that states the sheet's real dimensions and that columns and rows start at 0.

nodes.name: region
nodes.summary: Returns an arbitrary rectangle of the sheet (top-left x/y plus width and height) as a Bitmap. This is the counterpart to `cell` for packed sheets whose frames sit at explicit positions — an Aseprite export gives each frame's rectangle — rather than on a fixed grid.

nodes.name: slice
nodes.summary: Slices a sheet image into a grid of equal-size cells and returns a Sheet to pull cells from. It reads the picture at its own resolution so tiles come across pixel-exact, picks 3- or 4-byte pixels depending on whether transparency is honored, and verifies the byte count before building the Sheet.

nodes.name: load_sheet
nodes.summary: Loads a whole sheet image as a single-cell Sheet whose native size is the tile size, so callers can pull arbitrary rectangles with `Sheet#region`. Used for packed sheets whose frame positions come from a data file (an Aseprite export) instead of a fixed grid.

nodes.name: divides_evenly!
nodes.summary: Guardrail that a sheet's pixel size splits into whole tiles before any slicing happens. A non-positive tile size, or a picture that does not divide evenly, raises a teaching error naming both real sizes and the resulting fractional tile counts — because slicing anyway would shear every tile after the first.

nodes.name: load
nodes.summary: The main entry point: loads an image file and converts it to an exact width x height Bitmap of console colors. It delegates to the see-through variant when transparency is requested, otherwise folds each RGB triple down through Color.rgb8 so imported images match hand-written ones.

nodes.name: load_transparent
nodes.summary: The see-through variant of `load`: reads RGBA and turns each pixel's alpha into either its color (opaque enough) or the TRANSPARENT marker (below the threshold), so a cut-out background lets the game field show through instead of drawing a box.

nodes.name: verify_size!
nodes.summary: Guards against an adapter returning the wrong amount of pixel data by comparing the byte count to width x height x bytes-per-pixel. Catching the mismatch here turns what would otherwise surface much later as garbled pixels into a clear immediate error.

nodes.name: ImageMagick
nodes.summary: The adapter that turns an image file into raw pixels by driving the ImageMagick command line. It resolves and remembers whichever binary is available (`magick`, then the older `convert`), exposes RGB, RGBA and dimension queries, and reports a missing install in plain language with the exact command to run.

nodes.name: rgb_pixels
nodes.summary: Returns raw RGB888 bytes for an image resized and cropped to the requested size — width*height*3 bytes, row-major, top-left origin. Transparency is flattened onto white for a clean opaque import.

nodes.name: rgba_pixels
nodes.summary: Returns raw RGBA8888 bytes — the same pixels as `rgb_pixels` plus a fourth alpha byte each — keeping transparency (background none) so a cut-out's removed background can be made see-through.

nodes.name: dimensions
nodes.summary: Reads an image's own [width, height] from its header without loading any pixels. Sheet slicing needs this to know how the picture divides into tiles before it cuts, so the later request at that exact size is a no-op resize and no tile is ever squashed.

nodes.name: binary
nodes.summary: Resolves the ImageMagick command once and memoizes it, preferring version 7's `magick` over the older `convert`. When neither runs it raises the friendly BackendUnavailable error rather than leaking a raw "command not found".

nodes.name: extract
nodes.summary: The private workhorse behind both pixel readers: builds the ImageMagick argument list that resizes to cover the target box, center-crops the overflow to an exact rectangle, and writes raw 8-bit channels straight to stdout with no file header. A non-zero exit becomes an Error naming the file and ImageMagick's own message.

nodes.name: unavailable_error
nodes.summary: Builds the BackendUnavailable error raised when ImageMagick is not installed. The message says what happened and names the exact install command per platform (`brew install imagemagick`, `sudo apt-get install imagemagick`), matching the project's teaching-error style.

nodes.name: analyzer.rb
nodes.summary: Measures a built ROM's real per-frame cost on the emulator — the "analyze" half of the cost tooling, opposite the static estimate in IR::CostModel. `measure` boots a ROM, lets it settle, and reads how many of a frame's 228 scanlines the CPU actually burns; `profile` walks a game's scene dispatch and boots straight into each scene (by overriding the scene variable's boot value) so a scene reached only through input can still be measured without scripting button presses.
nodes.languageNotes: This file was missing from the project scan, so it never went through a file-analyzer batch. Its summary and its module/method structure were read directly from source during graph assembly.

nodes.name: Analyzer
nodes.summary: Module holding the measured half of the cost tooling. Where IR::CostModel estimates a frame's cost statically, Analyzer runs the real ROM on the emulator and reads how many of a frame's 228 scanlines the CPU actually burns. Holds the frame constants (FRAME_SCANLINES, SATURATED, SETTLE, SCENE_CAP) and the measure/profile entry points.

nodes.name: Analyzer::Result
nodes.summary: Immutable value object (Data.define) wrapping one measurement's scanline count, with helpers to ask whether the CPU was effectively maxed out for the frame and what share of the frame was consumed.

nodes.name: saturated?
nodes.summary: True when the measured scanlines reach the saturation threshold, meaning the CPU is effectively maxed for the frame. The emulator's reading caps and wobbles near the ceiling, so this is a 'saturated' verdict rather than an exact count.

nodes.name: percent
nodes.summary: The share of a full 228-scanline frame the measurement consumed, rounded to a whole percent — the human-readable form of the raw scanline count.

nodes.name: measure
nodes.summary: Runs a built ROM on the emulator and returns its measured per-frame cost. Lets the game settle for a few frames first so it reaches steady state, then takes the smallest of three reads to reject noisy samples. Always closes the probe.

nodes.name: profile
nodes.summary: Measures each of a game's scenes separately and returns a scene-name => Result hash. A game with no scenes is profiled as a whole. `only:` narrows to named scenes; otherwise every scene is profiled up to SCENE_CAP.

nodes.name: scenes
nodes.summary: Reads a game's scene dispatch out of its IR by finding the case node, returning the selector variable and a scene-name => value map. Returns nil when the game has no scenes and is just a single game loop.

nodes.name: pick_scenes
nodes.summary: Chooses which scenes to profile: the explicitly named ones, or all of them up to the cap when none are named. Raises a friendly error naming the game's real scenes when an unknown scene name is asked for.

nodes.name: boot_into
nodes.summary: Returns a throwaway copy of the program that boots straight into one scene, by overriding the scene variable's boot value — so a scene the player only reaches through input can be measured without scripting button presses. Measures the scene's baseline cost only: state a transition would normally set up is absent.

nodes.name: measure_program
nodes.summary: Lowers an IR program to a real ROM, writes it to a temporary file, and measures it — the bridge from an in-memory program to a number read off the emulator.

layers.name: DSL Surface
