layers.description: The Ruby game-writing API a user actually touches: the RubyGBA.build entry point, the Builder class with its themed verb mixins (drawing, sprites, tiled, input, audio, control flow), and the handle objects those verbs return (Value, Condition, Sprite, Pool, List, Grid, Table, Timer, fonts and the audio model) — the tier whose whole job is to hide GBA hardware behind names that read like game code.

layers.name: IR Core
layers.description: The target-agnostic intermediate representation the DSL builds instead of emitting code directly: the IR::Node op-tree model, the IR::Build constructors, the cross-backend contracts (Int32 wraparound semantics, screen size, button vocabulary), the well-formedness verifier, and the portable analysis passes (palette building, glyph tree-shaking, screen-mode resolution) — nothing here knows about ARM or the GBA.

layers.name: Guardrails & Cost Analysis
layers.description: The project's signature validation tier, which runs over the IR before any code exists: the guardrail registry plus sixteen checks that turn silent black-screen footguns (a missing screen mode, no VBlank wait, an orphaned condition, a redrawn frame, an overrun IWRAM budget) into friendly build-time errors, together with the static per-frame cost model, its calibrated op weights, and the report printer.

layers.name: Lowering Backends
layers.description: The two consumers of the IR tree, where all target-specific detail is confined: IR::Backends::GBA lowers a program to real ARM7 machine code across fourteen modules (drawing, audio, mixer, lists, timers, collision, save memory, two-pass emission) using the ARM instruction encoder and the GBA hardware register map, while IR::Backends::Ruby runs the same tree headlessly as the reference interpreter and test oracle.

layers.name: ROM Output & Verification
layers.description: The cartridge-image tier at the end of the pipeline: the ROM byte buffer and header writer, the structural doctor that rejects images the BIOS would refuse, the header/disassembly inspector and function dumper, the built-in diagnostic test-pattern ROMs, and the emulator seam plus pixel/audio verifier and per-frame cost analyzer that prove a finished ROM behaves.

layers.name: Asset Import Pipeline
layers.description: The host-side importers that turn real artist and audio files into data the console can use: PNG/JPG decoding into console colors through the pluggable image adapter that shells out to ImageMagick, the native Aseprite parser that reads layers, frames and named animations straight from the binary, and the WAV loader that converts any PCM file to the 8-bit mono samples the sampled-audio hardware plays.

layers.name: CLI & Developer Tooling
layers.description: The developer-facing commands and scripts around the library: the Thor-based ruby-gba CLI with its executable shim and the Game declaration registry it reads, plus the repo scripts that calibrate the cost model against the emulator, regenerate example art and audio, and render an interpreter run as a PNG preview.

layers.name: Example Games
layers.description: The runnable showcase and teaching programs written in the DSL itself — Pong, Breakout, Snake, Pac-Man, a shmup split across multiple files, a raycaster, plus focused demos of tiles, scrolling, parallax, sprite sheets, fonts and audio — together with the example assets and the generator that bakes them.

layers.name: Project Configuration & Docs
layers.description: Repository-level scaffolding: the gemspec, Gemfile and Rakefile that package the gem and drive the test task (including the vendored gemba-core C extension build), the README, agent contributor guide and license, the manually dispatched GitHub Actions test workflow, and the commit-msg hook that keeps tracker ids out of history.

tour.title: What writing a game feels like
tour.description: Start where a user starts, not where the compiler starts. `examples/snake.rb` is a complete Snake — a growing body, random food, a live score, a game-over screen — and it is written in nothing but plain Ruby: `list` for the body, `every` for the movement beat, `held(:up).then` for steering. The README frames why that is the whole point: this project is a teaching tool whose rule is that you should need to know Ruby, not the Game Boy Advance. Read this step as the destination, then spend the rest of the tour finding out how those words turn into a cartridge.
tour.languageLesson: The DSL is a Ruby block evaluated against a builder object (`RubyGBA.game(...) do ... end`), so every verb you see is just a method call on a hidden receiver. That is why game code reads like a language of its own while staying ordinary Ruby you can debug, `puts`, and unit-test.

tour.title: One require, one build call
tour.description: `lib/ruby_gba.rb` is the graph's hub — 41 outgoing requires and 35 files pointing back at it — because it is the require barrel that loads all forty modules of the framework and defines `RubyGBA.build`, the single call that turns a DSL block into a finished ROM. `game.rb` sits beside it and adds a deliberate split: `RubyGBA.game` only *records* a game in a registry without building anything, so the command-line tool can decide the output path and the reporting later. Every example and every tool in this repo begins by requiring this one file.
tour.languageLesson: Ruby's 'barrel' idiom: one file whose job is a list of `require_relative` lines in dependency order. It gives users a single entry point and gives the library one obvious place to see its own shape.

tour.title: The Builder and its verb mixins
tour.description: `Builder` is the object your `build` block is evaluated against, so every verb from Step 1 is one of its methods. Rather than one enormous class, it mixes in seventeen themed modules — drawing, sprites, control flow, input, audio, and more — which keeps the user-facing surface deliberately flat (you call `pixel` and `game_loop` side by side, never `builder.drawing.pixel`) while the source stays readable. Two of these are worth noting now: `drawing.rb` remembers which screen you picked, which is later what lets `sprite` choose its own implementation, and `control_flow.rb` owns `wait_vblank`, which is where the framework quietly repaints sprites and advances animations for you.
tour.languageLesson: Ruby modules as mixins let one class be assembled from many files without inheritance. `include` splices a module's methods into the class, so `Builder` can be split by topic for maintainers while presenting a single flat namespace to users.

tour.title: Handles: what the verbs hand back
tour.description: A DSL verb rarely just does something — it returns a small handle object you keep using, and these files define them. `var :x, 0` returns a `Value`, and because `Value` implements the ordinary Ruby operators, `x + 1` and `x > 240` build up an expression rather than computing a number: comparisons produce a `Condition`, `.then { }` produces a `Branch` still waiting for an optional `.else`. `Sprite` is a picture that owns its own position and leaves no smear behind it as it moves, and `Pool` is a fixed-capacity set of behaving things (bullets, enemies, particles) so a game never hand-manages parallel lists that fall out of step.
tour.languageLesson: This is operator overloading used to build a tree, not to compute. Ruby lets `+`, `>`, `&` and `|` be defined as methods, so `(hx < MIN) | (hx > MAX)` returns a composed `Condition` object. The same trick powers query builders and ORMs — deferred, inspectable expressions that something else executes later.

tour.title: The IR: a program as inspectable data
tour.description: Here is the pivot of the whole architecture. Instead of emitting machine code as it goes, the builder from Steps 3 and 4 grows an intermediate representation: a plain-Ruby op-tree of `IR::Node` objects that says *what the program does*, with nothing in it that assumes a Game Boy Advance. Control flow is real nesting, so there are no labels or jumps here — those are an artifact of flattening, and are left to whoever consumes the tree. `int32.rb` is the quiet hero: it pins signed 32-bit wraparound semantics once, as a contract, so two very different consumers cannot silently disagree about overflow or negative division.
tour.languageLesson: Building data first and interpreting it later is the classic compiler split, and it buys three things at once: you can validate a program before any code exists (Step 7), resolve forward references in a second pass (Step 9), and run the same program on more than one target (Step 10).

tour.title: The screen, without the jargon
tour.description: The console's screen is 240x160 pixels, and this is the only place that number is stated — the interpreter sizes its fake screen from it and the hardware constants derive from it. `modes.rb` handles a genuinely tricky idea: the machine can present a picture in more than one way (a plain grid of colored pixels, or a composition of small reusable tiles plus hardware-drawn sprites), and a routine reached from two different modes would draw the wrong way, so this file follows the call graph and raises a friendly conflict instead. `palette.rb` keeps the framework's central promise: some display modes store a small numbered table of colors rather than a color per pixel, so this file walks the finished program, collects every color name you used, and builds that table silently.
tour.languageLesson: The console stores a color in 15 bits (five each for blue, green and red) rather than the 24-bit RGB you are used to. `color.rb` hides that entirely: you write `:red` or `rgb8(200, 30, 30)` and it converts, validates the channel ranges, and hands the hardware its packed value.

tour.title: Guardrails: black screens become build errors
tour.description: This is the project's signature idea and the reason the IR exists. Learning this hardware is miserable because nearly every mistake produces the same silent black screen with no crash to point at — so sixteen checks walk the op-tree before any code is generated and turn each classic footgun into a friendly, plain-language build error with a suggested fix. The four here cover the worst offenders: a program that draws but never picked a display and so runs perfectly and invisibly (`screen_mode_set`), a loop that never waits for the screen refresh and therefore runs thousands of times a second instead of sixty (`vblank_sync`), the sprite that is missing because its whole footprint fell outside the screen (`off_screen_draw`), and a program that simply ends, leaving the console executing whatever garbage bytes follow it in memory (`termination`).
tour.languageLesson: The registry pattern: `guardrails.rb` holds only the mechanism (a list of checks, a validation pass, and `Finding`/`Fix` value objects), while each check is a small self-contained file that knows one piece of hardware lore. Adding a new check means adding a file, not editing a switch statement.

tour.title: Will it actually run at 60fps?
tour.description: The guardrails in Step 7 catch mistakes; the cost model catches a subtler failure — a game that is simply too slow. The console redraws the screen sixty times a second, and there is only a brief safe window each frame in which drawing does not tear the picture, so `cost_model.rb` estimates a program's per-frame work in scanlines before the ROM ever exists. Those estimates are not guesses: `measured_weights.rb` is a generated table calibrated against real hardware. `draw_budget` turns the estimate into a warning when a frame overflows, `frame_reach` answers 'what does this loop actually run every frame?' once for all the per-frame checks, and `analyzer.rb` closes the loop by measuring a built ROM's real cost on the emulator.

tour.title: Lowering to real ARM7 machine code
tour.description: Now the op-tree becomes a cartridge. The GBA backend walks the target-agnostic IR from Step 5 and emits actual ARM7 instructions, deciding along the way where each variable lives in the console's fast work memory and preparing every picture, tile map and color table in advance. It runs in two passes because of a chicken-and-egg problem: a jump forward lands at an address the backend has not written yet, so `emit.rb` writes each jump as a fixed-size placeholder and patches in the real distance once all positions are known. Beneath that, `asm.rb` encodes single instructions into raw bytes, `constants.rb` is the one file permitted to know raw hardware addresses, and `rom.rb` assembles the cartridge header — title, checksum, boot logo — and pads the image to a power of two.
tour.languageLesson: Two-pass assembly is the standard answer to forward references. Pass one emits code and records where each named position landed; pass two revisits every placeholder jump and fills in the now-known offset. It is the same idea as a linker's relocation table, at a smaller scale.

tour.title: The second backend: a headless oracle
tour.description: The same IR from Step 5 has a second consumer, and this is the unusual design decision worth pausing on. `backends/ruby.rb` interprets the op-tree directly in Ruby against simulated hardware — a fake framebuffer, a fake gamepad, an in-memory variable store, timers and a software audio mixer — so a test can build a program, run it, and assert a specific pixel or variable in-process, with no emulator and no ROM. The `int32.rb` contract from Step 5 is precisely what keeps the two backends agreeing on arithmetic, and `portability.rb` tags each op kind as portable or hardware-only so a preflight can say up front that a program uses an escape hatch, rather than a backend exploding halfway through.
tour.languageLesson: A reference interpreter beside a real code generator is a differential-testing setup: run one program through both and any disagreement is a bug in one of them. The interpreter is also thousands of times faster to start than an emulator, which is what makes it usable as the default test oracle.

tour.title: Bringing real art and sound in
tour.description: A teaching framework is no fun if all the art has to be typed as ASCII, so this small layer converts files an artist actually made into data a cartridge can hold. `image.rb` turns a PNG or JPG into a flat list of console colors, handling alpha cutouts and slicing sprite or tile sheets into equal cells, all behind a swappable adapter. `aseprite.rb` goes further and reads the native binary format of a popular pixel-art editor directly — layers, frames, palette, frame durations, and named animations — so a game can point straight at the artist's saved file with no export step. `wav.rb` does the audio equivalent, converting any WAV into the 8-bit mono samples the sound hardware plays.
tour.languageLesson: The adapter pattern draws a hard line around an external dependency: `image_magick.rb` is the single file in this project that shells out to an image tool. Everything else talks to the adapter interface, so swapping or stubbing the tool touches exactly one file.

tour.title: Closing the feedback loop
tour.description: The tour ends with the tooling that makes the whole pipeline usable, because fast mechanical feedback is an explicit goal of this project. `bin/ruby-gba` is a thin shim that puts the working copy's `lib/` on the load path and hands off to the Thor-based CLI, which builds a declared game, inspects a ROM, scaffolds a starter file, and reports measured per-frame cost. `tools/preview.rb` runs a program on the Step 10 interpreter and writes a self-contained HTML page that replays the captured frames on a canvas, so scrolling and animation can be watched with no emulator at all. `verifier.rb` is the opposite end of the same question — it boots the real ROM and reads back the pixels it truly rendered — and the CI workflow runs both suites on demand.
tour.languageLesson: YAML CI: this GitHub Actions workflow uses `workflow_dispatch` only — no `push` or `pull_request` trigger — so it gates nothing automatically and runs on demand. It installs a C toolchain, libmgba and ImageMagick first, because the emulator-backed tests build a native extension rather than skipping when the emulator is missing.
